Rt. Hon. Sir WILFRID, LAURIER (Prime Minister). Some time ago the hon. the leader of the opposition made inquiry as to the waterways treaty which is now being considered by the Senate of the United States. I told my hon. friend we would communicate with the home authorities, and I have to-day the authority of His Excellency the Governor General to give to the House the despatch which His Excellency has received on this subject from the Earl of Crewe, the Colonial Secretary. The despatch reads:
London, January 29, 1909.
I am in receipt of your telegram of January 28, and from your telegram of January 9, I gather that your responsible advisers have the full text of the treaty before them.
According to press reports there seems to be some misunderstanding as to the presentation of the treaty to the Dominion parliament.
In this country the treaty-making power is the King, acting on the advice of his responsible ministers, who in cases of treaties which affect a Dominion Act of course in full consultation and accord with the government of the Dominion concerned.
In the United States the treaty-making power is with the advice and consent of the Senate, and until the Senate of the United States of America approve of any treaty it is not the practice to publish or present to parliament either in this country or in Canada, or to publish in the United States or to present to congress. The fact that the Senate of the United States see the treaty before the parliament of the Dominion, but not before government of the Dominion, is therefore entirely due to the terms of the constitution of the United States.
I am in hopes that your responsible advisers will clearly explain this to parliament, and will point out that the relation between the parliament of the Dominion and the government of the Dominion in this respect is practically analogous to that between the Imperial parliament and the government of His Majesty the King.
(Sgd.) CREWE.

REID (Grenville) moved second reading of Bill (No. 2) to amend the Passenger Tickets Act. He said :	Last
year I presented this Bill in exactly the same form, but the Prime Minister did not wish it to go to the committee on account

of the absence of the Minister of Railways.	The Bill proposes to add two
clauses to the Passenger Tickets Act. In this bill I ask that the mileage book issued by the railway companies should be good on their trains. At present if a passenger has purchased a thousand mile book and presents it on the train, the conductor cannot take the number of miles off, but has to insist on the passenger paying for a ticket. All that the owner of a book can do is to get a ticket in exchange at the station for the number of miles torn off by the agent. On the other side of the line, they issue these books, but there these books are good on the trains. I claim that when a railway company sells a mileage book, that book ought to be valid on the train as well as at the station. In Canada the railway companies charge 21 cents per mile for their mileage books. On the other side of the line they charge 2 cents per mile; and I understand that some of the American railway companies which run trains partly through Canada, issue mileage books, which are good in Canada, at 2 cents per mile. It seems to me that our railway companies should reduce the rate to 2 cents per mile for these mileage books, and if necessary limit the duration of these books to a certain time. This matter is one which I would like the Railway Committee to discuss. Another clause in this Bill deals with the interchange of tickets from union stations. There are a number of stations in Canada which are called union stations because they are used by more than one railway company. Often the trains of different companies start almost at the same time and passengers are apt to take the wrong train. A passenger who has bought a ticket by the Canadian Pacific Railway will sometimes take the Grand Trunk Raii-way by mistake, and the conductor of course cannot accept his ticket. My suggestion is that if any one should happen to get on the wrong train, going to the same point, the conductor should accept his ticket, and the company would then collect from the other company who sold it. It may be said that if the passenger has the money, there is no reason why he should not buy a ticket and collect the other one from the other company. But it takes two or three months to get the money back, and often the passenger may find it almost impossible to collect it. He may be living at New York and may take the train in Toronto for Montreal and take a Canadian Pacific Railway train instead of a Grand Trunk Railway or vice versa. If he had purchased a Canadian Pacific Railway ticket and then by mistake took the Grand Trunk Railway train, there is no reason why the conductor should not accept that ticket and hand it to the company who would in turn collect the amount from the Canadian Pacific Railway. This would not cause the companies Mr. J. D. REID.
any great inconvenience, because every day they are selling tickets on which they must collect the money from one another. For instance, I purchase a ticket at Toronto for Ottawa. Half the trip is on the Canadian Pacific Railway, and the Canadian Pacific Railway have to collect from the Grand Trunk Railway the amount from Brockville to Ottawa. My proposition therefore will not impose on these companies any extra trouble worth mentioning. I have in my mind a case in which a woman got on a train in Toronto bound for Montreal. It was a night train. She had a Canadian Pacific Railway ticket and by mistake she got on the Grand Trunk Railway train. She had not enough money to pay for another ticket so that the conductor had to put her off at Port Hope. She was taken back to Toronto and had to stay there until the next morning so that she could not get to Montreal until the next night. This was a great inconvenience, especially as this woman had been called to Montreal on account of sickness in her family. I can see no reason why the Grand Trunk Railway should not have accepted her ticket and then collected the amount from the Canadian Pacific Railway.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Does my hon. friend know of any other case?

I have heard of others but I do not suppose there are manv. There are, however, some in which the hardships are. very great. It is easy for a passenger to take the wrong train, and these mistakes are made generally by persons who may not have the money, to purchase other tickets. These are points I would like the Railway Committee to consider and discuss. I do not want to take up the time discussing the question, as we can do that much better in committee. The right hon. the Prime Minister gave a good reason last year why he could not allow it to go to the committee, but now that the Minister of Railways is here (Mr. Graham) I would ask the right hon. gentleman to let the Bill go to the Railway Committee.

speakeroldname: Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways).
speechtext:
I am not sure that we ought to hold the railway companies responsible for the mistakes which the rest of us make. While there is something in the contention of my hon. friend, I presume that there is no very extensive grievance through people getting on the wrong train with the right ticket. If the great body of the public were in the same position as my hon. friend and myself, it would make no difference to them which train they got on, but unfortunately for them they are not in that happy condition. The trouble possibly arises primarily in the fact that the stations are not constructed as they ought to be for great traffic. In a properly constructed and conducted union station of large pro-

portions, it is almost impossible for a passenger to get on a wrong train because he cannot get in or where the wrong train is. As regards the question of mileage books being honoured on the trains, there is room for argument and I would like to Imar some discussion of it by the Railway Committee.
1	have had conductors on Canadian trains honour my mileage coupons and I think the order which provides that they do not accept the mileage coupons except at the station, if it exists, must be of recent date However, that is worthy of discussion. There may be reasons of convenience and safety to the companies which justify such an order.
As to the question of thS rate at which the books ought to be issued, I stated last night that the Canadian parliament has adopted a course with reference to the control of rates through a Board of Railway Commissioners, both as to freight and passengers, and I believe we ought, at least for the present, to give that board a fair trial hi the arrangement and adjustment of rates, both passenger and freight. If there be any hardship, any reason why passenger rates should be reduced from one point to any other point, the Board of Railway Commissioners has full power under the Act to hear that complaint and adjudicate upon it. When it is said the railways of Canada must give a mileage book rate of 2 cents per mile, it is well known, particularly in a new country, that there are parts of these railway lines, and the entire road of some companies, that could not stand a rate of
2	cents per mile; but parliament, in its wisdom, has placed these matters in the hands of a Board of Railway Commissioners, deputing them to adjust the rates in different parts of the country according to the conditions that exist in that part of the country. There are some sections on new roads where it would be very unjust and unwise to tie the company down to a rate that might be perfectly fair on some other part of that same line or on some other line, and the difference of conditions existing in different parts of the country has led parliament to place this control of rates in the hands of a Board of Railway Commissioners, and I might say to my hon. friend that I am willing to have some other parts of the Bill discussed in the Railway Committee, and cannot say that this part shall not be discussed, I set my face against that part of it and say that the government could not consent to changing our policy in that direction. If there is any complaint the board has been established for the purpose of adjudicating upon such a complaint.
There may be some difference of opinion in the committee as to this interchange of tickets. My hon. friend has referred to the fact that one line now collects a rate
for another line, but there is this difference: The line on which the traffic originates has a joint traffic arrangement with the line with which it connects and they divide the receipts pro rata according to their joint tariff arrangement. Under this proposition there is no joint tariff arrangement because under the system suggested, the Grand Trunk, for instance, if it sold a ticket, would simply originate the ticket and would have the contract, and it would work out that the road that originated the tiaffic would pay a percentage to the road that completed the traffic for collection and its part of the freight, and we would find here that the road that sold the ticket and got no profit would have to pav the road that did not sell the ticket, but got all the profit for collecting its ticket. You could not make that work in practice unless you could make the law work backwards in this particular case. My own view is that it would be difficult to work. I have had some experience in selling tickets in the past. The ticket seller has to make his returns daily; the conductor takes up a certain number of tickets and his collections must correspond eventually with the ticket seller's report of tickets for that day. If we allowed that mixing up of tickets and required one railway to honour the tickets of another railway, we would interfere a good deal with the rights of these companies and the contracts they make with the passengers.
Having said this much and explained my position in regard to the price of mileage tickets, I have no objection to having this Bill go to the Railway Committee for discussion, without committing myself to any part of the Bill.

I agree with the Minister of Railways that the matter of the rates might perhaps as well be left to the Railway Commission. The minister has not dealt with the clause requiring the conductor to accept these mileage tickets. If a man once pays his money to any agent of the company, why should he have to exchange the tickets he thus buys for any other ticket? The railways sell these tickets for their own benefit, and having sold them that sale should be final. I would think that principle of the Bill ought to be sustained.
There is some need for the part of the Bill compelling a railway to honour the ticket of another railway whose trains start from the same station, as in the case of the Union station in Toronto. I have often seen people put off the train at South Park-dale because they had tickets of the other line. The trains leave at nearly the same time and there should be some protection for people who take the wrong train, par-

ticularly as the trains of the same railway do not always leave from the same platform. It might be advisable to enact that where the trains leave the same station within half an hour of each other the tickets of the other line should be honoured. The railways could honour each other's tickets in this way and adjust their accounts at the end of the month as they do in other matters. In some parts of the country there is an evil such as is sought to be remedied by clause 7b of this Bill.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time.

On the order:
Second reading of Bill (No. 3) to amend the Railway Act.-Mr. Bickerdike.

I understand that, under the arrangement arrived at just before the adjournment of the House last evening, it will be impossible for me to go on with this Bill, as the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham), has taken us into his confidence and informed us that he intends to bring down a Bill to cover this case. Had this Bill gone on, I should have desired to propose an amendment in the form of additional clauses. With the permission of the House, I will read these clauses, which I commend to the favourable consideration of the Minister of Railways. My contention is that the whole of this matter should come under the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission. They are the only people, I think, who can deal with it intelligently. Therefore, I would have proposed to introduce the following:
2.	All highway crossings at rail 'level shall he constructed, protected and maintained in accordance with the orders and regulations of the board.
3.	The board may determine what highway crossings at rail level, now used, are, in its opinion, dangerous, and thereupon the board may direct the company to change the curve of the railway at such crossings, or alter the approaches thereto, or erect gates thereat, or make such other changes as the board deems necessary for the protection of persons using such crossings. Provided that no company shall be required to make such changes in any one year at more than twenty-five per cent of the crossings upon its railway which are determined by the board to be dangerous.
2. The board may direct at which of such dangerous crossings the necessary changes shall be made during the first year and so on in each succeeding year until all such dangerous crossings have been so changed.
I hope that this principle will be incorporated in any measure on the subject that is adopted.
That can stand as a notice. Stand.

Mr. ROBERT BICKERDIKE (St. Lawrence, Montreal) moved the second reading of Bill (No. 4) to amend the Criminal Code. He said: As I said, when I introduced this Bill, the object is to add to the number of cases in which the lash may be used. The first is for those who carry concealed weapons and use them on the slightest provocation. The next is in the case of assault upon females. The section says:
Every one is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to three years imprisonment, and to be whipped, who assaults his wife or other female and thereby occasions actual bodily harm.
The Bill provides the same in the case of those guilty of robbery; and the fourth case is that of assault with intent to rob-highway robbery. In my opinion, in all these cases, the judge should be given discretion to sentence the offender to the lash as well as to imprisonment.

speakeroldname: Hon. A. B. AYLESWORTH (Minister of Justice).
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Before the second reading is carried, I would like to say a word on the general subject adverted to by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bickerdike) who has introduced the measure. In doing so, I wish to be understood as expressing the individual opinions on the subject which I myself hold, and as not desiring that those opinions should carry any especial weight except such as my position as one of the members of this House might involve. I am opposed to the whole principle of inflicting punishment upon criminals by the use of the lash. I regard it merely as a survival of the days of primitive man, when the * only canon of punishment known was the law of retaliation, which exacted an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth, a life for a life. In later days, days which, while not within living memory, are not yet so far gone by, the principle of retaliation seemed still to survive in regard to many offences known to the British law. In the days of the Stuarts punishment by the infliction of personal pain was the rule, perhaps, rather than the exception, and we read of the use of instruments of torture. We see these instruments of torture preserved in our museums, and we think ourselves better than our forefathers, who applied the rack or the thumbscrew or the boot, or other means of inflicting bodily pain upon those who had offended against the law or who were charged with some such offence. We consider ourselves, in modern days, to have become more civilized, to have attained truer ideas of the principles upon which punishment legally and judicially imposed for offences against the criminal law ought to be administered. And yet the principle, or practice, of flogging for certain offences still applies, and provisions that it may be

the means of punishment still appear upon our statute-book. I am not proposing that there should be alterations; I am not prepared to set up my individual opinion against the opinions of very many men thoroughly as well able to form sound judgment upon this subject as I can be, and I am not proposing to amend the Criminal Code by reducing the number of cases in which whipping may be administered. But there are serious practical difficulties in the way of carrying out the law as it now stands in the few cases in which whipping is a part of the punishment which the law prescribes. One practical question is: Who is to be the official who shall administer this punishment? The judge adds to his sentence of so many months, or so many years, imprisonment-quite as an off-hand matter, it may be-a provision that the prisoner shall be flogged once, or twice, or it may be three times, during the course of his sentence. That is all the court does in the matter; no directions are given, but it is left to the officers of the law to carry out the sentence of the court. The prisoner goes to some jail, or prison, or penitentiary, and the responsibility for seeing that the sentence is carried out rests upon the head of that institution.
The warden of the penitentiary sees perhaps for the first time when the prisoner arrives accompanied by the warrant of commitment, that flogging is to be administered to this man. Is the warden himself to handle the knout, or is he to delegate that duty to one of his subordinate officials ; and if to one of them, is the warden to select the man who shall carry out the sentence of the court ? In practice the matter is reduced to that. The warden has to nominate some one of his subordinate officials and instruct that man, putting I suppose the instrument of punishment into his hands, to lay the lash on the bare back of the prisoner. That punishment will be either a farce, a perfect mockery, or it will be something so terrible to think about that it ought, I think, to give any one concerned in the infliction of such punishment, or in ordering it, pause before he pronounces the words [DOT] that would condemn any fellow human being to such degradation, and to a punishment of that description. It all depends upon the willingness of the executioner, upon the amount of energy he puts into his right arm when he lays on the blows. The punishment may be a farce, or it may be something terrible to contemplate. I suppose it is intended to be a real thing, that it is meant to be a whipping laid on with all the strength that the warden or guard of the penitentiary who may be willing to administer it, can put into his blows.
I do not discuss the moral effect upon the man who administers the punishment.
I think, to say the least of it, that it cannot be an elevating effect. I do not wonder when I find that many and many a man who has accepted a position as guard or warden, or police official in our penitentiaries, says,, when ordered to administer a whipping, this is not within my contract,
I did not come into the public service of Canada to be a quasi executioner. It accordingly reduces itself in practice simply to what I say, that there are some particular guards in the penitentiaries who are willing to do this thing ; there are others who are unwilling, and we have to select such means as we can find. In the custody of our prisoners in penitentiaries or in jails no matter, I may say, how highly the prison offence which they may commit would seem to deserve the lash, no matter though the offence may be one of such an effect upon the other convicts as practically to destroy the whole discipline of the institution, no matter though the offence may be one arising out of pure ugliness on the part of the convict the lash is not used. We have upon occasion, and in extreme cases, used an instrument of punishment best described by the word paddle, and with which we administered a sound snanking upon the convict. I see a considerable difference between the two things. The lash is designed to tear the flesh, to bring blood; the other instrument will at least leave no external sign of injury. At times we punish in our penitentiaries by turning the hose upon the prisoner, in a confined cell so that he cannot escape when the water is turned on. We find that a very effective punishment indeed. It produces discomfort. It may be that at the time of the infliction it produces more or less of a sensation which might properly be described as pain, but it produces no ill effects. For my part, and for every reason, I state myself to be entirely opposed to the principle of punishing an offence against our laws by something which is literally nothing but an infliction of bodily pain.
It is said that there is a kind of fitness, a kind of special propriety, in punishment of this sort for offences against women. There might be other punishment suggested that would seem to be even more proper. No man I suppose, in this House or out of it, would seriously suggest the mutilation of an offender against these laws; and yet in conversation men say to one another at times that that would be the proper punishment. Is there any difference in principle ? There may be a difference in degree; but so far as I am concerned, each proposition seems to me to rest substantially upon the same principle for its foundation.	.
In regard to this particular measure which has been proposed by my hon. friend, four specific offences are mentioned as those which he proposes to add to the list of

crimes already mentioned in the Criminal Code for which whipping may be inflicted by the presiding judge, or the presiding magistrate, who disposes of the charge. The possession of a deadly weapon is one, also assaults, not assaults of the character which are commonly spoken of as criminal assaults, indecent assaults, but the ordinary assault and battery of a man beating a woman. Then highway robbery, or assaults with intent to commit highway robbery. Now taking these in turn, I may say to my hon. friend that so far as the offence of carrying a deadly weapon is concerned, my views go entirely with his own. I see no justification whatever in this country for a man carrying upon his person about the streets a weapon which can only be used for purposes of offence. A knife may be a deadly weapon, a razor in the hands of a desperate man may be a most deadly weapon. But these are. generally instruments of usefulness. I would not be disposed to extend to the carrying of instruments of that character the special punishment which my hon. friend is proposing here, or any special punishment. The carrying of a dirk or dagger, a weapon that may be used only for the purposes of stabbing, is altogether a different story. But even in that case, while every one would, I think, agree, while certainly I would agree, to the fullest extent with the views of my hon. friend that the carrying of such weapons ought to be made punishable, I would not be willing to add to the imprisonment the punishment of whipping. So with regard to the offences of highway robbery, robbery with violence, or an assault with intent to commit such robbery.
1 am perfectly aware that, as a matter of record, the offence of garrotting at one time became so prevalent in England, in London particularly, that extreme measures had to be resorted to in order to stamp it out, and the punishment of whipping was prescribed. That was carried out by the judges, and as a consequence the crime of garrotting was in a short time at an end and no longer known in that portion of the world. But I may concede to my hon. friend, or to any one who advocates the application of whipping to offences of the character of highway rob-berv or assaults with intent, that if there were such an unusual condition of things in any community in this country as seemed to call for very special and extreme measures of repression, whipping might be for a time used as a means of putting an end to what might be called an outbreak or epidemic of the character T am referring to.
But, I know of no ground for believing that any such condition of things does, at the present time, exist anywhere in Canada. In conversation my hon. friend mentioned to me the prevalence of offences of this sort in certain portions of Montreal, and I have Mr. AYLESWOKTH.
been unable to avoid noticing, in reading the files of prisoners' cases, of applicants for clemency during the last few months, or during the time that I have been in charge of the Justice Department, that these offences did seem to be more prevalent in the city of Montreal than anywhere else in Canada. There are more frequent convictions for offences of that character apparently in Montreal than in Toronto or any other of our larger cities. But there have been no representations made to the department from judges, juries, or other quarters that the offence of assaulting with intent to commit highway robbery, or the actual commission of highway robbery, has become so rife in Montreal or anywhere else in the country that such special, extreme measures to repress it are necessary and in the absence of such representations I certainly feel myself unable to go with my hon. friend to the extent of enacting that such offences, wherever committed in Canada, should henceforth be punishable, at the will of the presiding magistrate, by the use of the lash.
There remains the offence of assault and battery where a woman is the victim of it, and in this regard I will admit that the application of the law of retaliation, (because it simply comes to that) is more justifiable because the apparent fitness of things seems to make it more proper, or less improper, to demand whipping as a part of the punishment than in any of the other instances that my hon. friend has selected in the measure now under consideration. I have, even in regard to offences of this character, the feeling which I have already expressed. I think that simple imprisonment ought to be, and would be, in all ordinary cases, a sufficient punishment for the beating of a woman by a man, but the offender is one for whom no man worthy of the name would have any sympathy and whom no man would wish to protect. I certainly do not wish to stand here as the defender of such a man. I am prepared to offer no opposition to my hon. friend's measure in so far as the second clause is concerned, making any one convicted of an offence of the character described against a woman liable to be sentenced to flogging. I certainly think that even in such cases sentence to such a punishment ought to be sparingly pronounced, but there may be cases in which it is the only way to protect our women from the assault and beating of a husband, or, it may be, of a father. At any rate if my hon. ifriend is willing to limit the provisions of his Bill to the second clause, I shall offer no opposition to it, but as far as the other clauses are concerned, while I speak, as I say, my own sentiments alone, and am sneaking for no other member of this House than myself,
I am opposed entirely to the position of my hon. friend.

Mr. Speaker, I am surprised and sorry that the hon. member for North York (Mr. Aylesworth) has expressed the opinions that he has just delivered himself of in this House. I am glad to know that it is solely as the member for North York that he has spoken. My opinion is that his expressions still may do harm, as he is also the Minister of Justice for Canada. I consider that a man who is brutal enough to commit any of the brutish crimes which are outlined in the Bill of my hon. friend for Montreal (Mr. Bickerdike) should be punished in a physical way, in the only way that will affect him. One of the main reasons that the hon. member for North York has stated for not inflicting this punishment i3 that he cannot get any one to inflict it. That is a matter of detail and we need not discuss it here. Otherwise we might say that a man should not be hanged because we cannot get any one to hang him. I congratulate the hon. member for Montreal on his Bill and I hope it will carry; crimes of the class in question are rampant and must be put down.

Mr. Speaker, I merely rise to express my dissent from the propositions laid down by the Hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Ayles-worth). The Minister of Justice, in his remarks, spoke and I think very properly and very naturally from the standpoint of the criminal, but he uttered not one single word from the standpoint of the unfortunate victim. I have always understood that in all penal legislation the one great thing was the defence of the inoffensive portion of the community. If it be true that offences of this character are being committed in this country, if it be true that the existing means of punishment have proved insufficient to prevent such offences, then I think this House should be prepared to resort to any means that may be necessary to protect the women of this country. I quite agree with all that the Minister of Justice says against the punishment that may degrade a man. I believe that it was a disgrace to the British navy that flogging existed to the extent to which it did, because we all know that the British seamen were, on the whole, a noble band of men, but I fail to see how a brute such as the one of whom we read in the papers the other day, convicted of an offence against his own daughter, a girl of 18, could be degraded by any punishment that could be inflicted. I desire to say that I shall support the Bill of the hon. member as it is, not for a moment as a matter of vengeance, not at all in order to be vindictive, but simply as the surest and best means of putting a stop to these offences. The Minister of Justice himself must admit that in cases of extreme emergency the very course suggested would be a course sufficient to wipe out such an offence as this. Therefore, on behalf of the inoffensive portion of the community, the women and children of this land, I am prepared to support this legislation. In fact, I would go a step further and say that I have often felt that the provision on the statute-book applicable to this offence is really for the benefit of the lazy loafer. As perhaps every man in this House and every lawyer knows a man unwilling to work is supported by an honest, industrious wife until patience ceases to be a virtue and he is taken to court. She lays a complaint and the husband is punished by sending him to the county jail where, all during the winter, he lives in comfort and luxury, while the poor woman that he has sworn to support is obliged to go out and support herself and her family. If the hon. gentleman would introduce another clause to provide that those men who failed to support their wives and children should not be rewarded by being sent to the county jail where they will not have to work, but would be given an adequate punishment it would have the effect of compelling them to do their duty in this regard.

My hon. friend from Hastings (Mr. Northrup) has not apprehended the remarks of my hon. friend the Minister of Justice. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice said in his opening remarks that he was simply expressing his own opinion and his own opinion was that he was against the suggested punishment of flogging in all eases, but he stated that in so far as offences against women were concerned he left this clause to the judgment of the House. He expressed his own opinion but he did not go any further. He presented objections which I think, are worthy of consideration with regard to the other disposition of the Bill which concerned offences there described, such as garrotting which was at one time prevalent in England. But, there is a class of beings who beat their wives and they deserve no sympathy from anybody. I would have no compunction whatever in giving the man who beats his wife or who beats a female a taste of his own medicine. However, when the Bill gets to committee it will be for hon. members to consider whe->
ther they are prepared to apply the lash for the other cftences described in the Bill. For my part I would hesitate to say that a man who carries a concealed weapon should be whipped, or even that a man who commits such a heinous offence as robbery should be subjected to the lash. We all remember that some years ago the offence known as garrotting was so prevalent in the city cf London that the magistrates asked that the lash be applied for that offence, and the law having passed in a very short time afterwards the offence disappeared.

which shows that the passage of such a severe law may have a very salutory effect in suppressing certain offences. I do not know that at the present time the offence is so prevalent in the city of Montreal-where it seems to be more prevalent than elsewhere-as to warrant such an extreme measure as inflicting the lash. I think this Bill should be read a second time and then go to committee so as to further elicit the opinion of the House. I repeat that I think my hon. friend from Hastings did not quite apprehend the views of the Minister of Justice who merely suggested that it should be left to the House to determine what should be done.

(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, I did not expect that this bill would come to-day for its second reading. This is not meant as a reproach against my hon. friend from Montreal (St. Lawrence). On the contrary, I acknowledge that he was entitled to press with the utmost expedition a piece of legislation which he holds as good. Therefore, 1 will not deal with this question; I merely intend putting upon record my disapproval of the proposal which the hon. member for St. Lawrence has just put forth.
We often hear it said that we live in a progressive era. Then, I think it would be a backward move to pass this measure.
I was pleased to hear the Minister of Justice saying that, as a matter of principle, he is opposed to this bill. Such an attitude on his part is consistent with that spirit of toleration which in my opinion is the liberal tenet. At the same time, it seemed to me that the statements put forth by the hon. member West Huron (Mr. Lewis) and the hon. member from East Hastings (Mr. Northrup) who have dealt with this question from the opposite side were tainted with the spirit of former days.
The hon. member for St. Lawrence no doubt seeks a most praiseworthy result, that is the betterment of men, but is he positive that he will achieve his end by those violent means?
I contend that the enforcement of such a punishment renders him who undergoes it an irreconcilable foe to society; Now then such cannot be the aim of society which has the least interest in bringing about that result.
That punishment is not only a disgrace for the culprit, but the dishonour is shared by the members of his family. That is unjust, still it is so. Public opinion will overlook and forget the jail and the penitentiary, but it will not overlook such a punishment. It looks upon it as upon the death penalty. Recent events have justified my fears on that point. A man was hanged. He left behind him a brother and two nephews who were leading a quiet and honest life in Montreal. The nephews were Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
two good natured workmen in a manufacture and were surrounded by the esteem and good will of their fellow-workers. Immediately after the hanging they were the butt of the most offensive and cruel remarks. They could not but be morally affected by such a situation. They, found work elsewere but they were again tormented in their new employment. The result was that being constantly wronged, they became wrong-doers themselves and now they are both in the penitentiary.
Some will say that this is an exceptional case, but I rather think that it is an instance of what happens unfortunately too often. Therefore I contend' that upon no account has society the right to do such an injury to people who are no offenders against its laws, especially when it has for its own protection other means which do not involve such lamentable results. To achieve that end society can rely on the jail and the penitentiary which ought to afford enough protection to the community.
I maintain that the existing legislation countenancing that ignominious punishment ought not to be tolerated any longer. However we are now discussing the proposal put forth by the hon. member for St. Lawrence and I must content myself with impugning it. The disgracing punishment by the lash has a demoralising influence upon the man who undergoes it, so that he cannot pluck up his courage and become an honest man again. That is a sufficient reason to reject it. Moreover I think that, the hon. Minister of Justice antagonizing this proposal, we shall hear no more about it.

speakeroldname: Mr. JAMES W. MADDIN (South Cape Breton).
speechtext:
The Minister of Justice, in reviewing this Bill, has said a great deal in which I concur. I agree with the hon. gentleman in all that he said with regard to the infliction of punishment, and I think the member for Hastings misunderstood the Minister of Justice, because as the Criminal Code now stands whipping is provided for all offences of an indecent nature committed against women.
However, when it comes to imposing corporal punishment for such offences as carrying concealed weapons or wife-beating, I submit that in doing this we are returning to the days of barbarism. Before hon. members vote on this measure, they should bear in mind that, under our criminal law, power is vested in the magistrates to summarily try cases of certain offences, such as indecent assaults and wife-beating, and the punishment in such cases' is of a very arbitrary nature. In our Penitentiaries Act it is provided that persons condemned to imprisonment for less than two years may be confined in a county jail and not be sent to penitentiary at all. Within recent years, in many of our municipalities,

where hard labour is imposed, the prisoners are obliged to work on the public highway. In a number of counties in the province from which I come, the judges in cases where imprisonment may be imposed for two years, are in the habit of making the term 12, 15 or 18 months in the county jail of the county where the offence was committed. Thus if the lash is to be applied for these various offences, the Bill will go further than its mover contemplated. The duty is not then cast on the warden of the penitentiary but on the keeper of the county jail and the sheriff of the municipality, and I submit that these are men of considerable refinement and good breeding and it would be exceedingly repugnant to them to take up the lash and apply it to the back of one of their fellow creatures.
This is not a new question by any means. For a number of years it has been agitated throughout the leading law publications, both on this side of the Atlantic and the other, and the consensus of opinion seems to be that it is not wise to return to the lash for trifling offences. In fact the majority of authorities are of the opinion that it is unwise to apply the lash in any case. As regards that part of the Act which punishes a man for wife-beating, I wonder what the mover of the Bill has to say about the woman who beats her husband.
I would say, serves him right.

As a matter of fact, if sta tistics were well and intelligently collected throughout the length and breadth of the country, while the records would not show as many cases of husbands beating wives as of wives beating husbands, still there are a number of such cases. I agree with my hon. friend from Hastings (Mr. Northrup) in having no regard for the man who strikes a woman under any provocation. But my hon. friend has taken but one view of the case. I have no regard or sympathy for the man who hangs about the house, a drunken loafer, living by the earnings of his wife. But what about the diligent hard working man who works eight or ten hours per day, and when he comes home finds his supper not ready, his children not washed and his wife gallivanting about the country. What is sauce for the goose might very well be sauce for the gander, and the mover of this measure might well be asked to incorporate in it husband as well as wife beating.
There is another very serious objection. So long as those who administer the laws of the land do not look with favour on a particular statute, that statute will not be successfully applied. I do not think it is to the discredit of our judges to say that the majority, in cases where whippings are imposed are very loath to impose it. As a matter of fact the punishment is optional just as it is in this Bill, and in a large number of cases the judges are very loath to impose it. In my short experience where I reside, I only recall three instances in which the lash was imposed, and for some reason or other it was not in? these cases applied. What will be the result if legislation of this kind be adopted? If the lash is not applied now in cases where it may be imposed, it is not more likely to be applied when imposed in more trifling cases, and a law which is not enforced will be looked upon by the criminal as so much dead wood which he need not take into account. Therefore I say that while the lash may have a tendency to lessen the outbreaks of crime of a certain violent character, I have no doubt that the diet described in Oliver Twist, which was supplied in the parochial workhouse, and the other rigours of that workhouse would be sufficient deterrents in cases of a less serious character, such as are dealt with in this measure.

NANTEL (Terrebonne.) (Translation.) Mr. Speaker, I shall say but one word on the question which is now before the House. I entirely agree with the hon. Minister of Justice on this point. In the first place I do not think that the circumstances prevailing in Montreal, for instance, would justify such a measure. I hope that we shall never go back to the barbarous ages, which in my opinion would be the result of this measure. The offence however odious, for which flogging is intended as a punishment, is after all but a mere misdemeanour, therefore it is more or less serious.
As a matter of principle, I am in favour of the death penalty, although I am entirely adverse to flogging. I will say more, I would favour the wiping of that punishment out of otir criminal code. With still more reason, I cannot approve of it in such a case as this when there is no motive to enforce it as the offence is not serious enough. Therefore I hope that this legislation will never become a part of our criminal law.

I am largely in accord with the hon. Minister of Justice as to this Bill. The fact that the majority of the lawyers in this House are opposed to such clause is one reason why I favour it, because that is an indication to me that it will have the effect of decreasing offences of that character and there will be less work in the courts for some lawyers. My hon. friend from Cape Breton (Mr. Maddin) put the question why there should not be some provision for the protection of men. Well, the man who goes to his home and is beaten once by his wife and then is foolish enough to go back, deserves to be beaten the second time.
That is not the case with the poor wo-

man; she has to stay at home all the time, she has frequently to submit to abuse in order to care for her children. The man at whom this punishment is aimed is the very man who will frequently trouble and bother such a woman, disturb her and her family and eat the food which she has provided by her day's hard work for her children. Therefore I am quite in accord with the punishment proposed. I am quite sure that the difficulties in connection with the infliction of the whipping can be overcome. We cannot be too careful or too severe in this particular, and while I agree with the Minister of Justice in all the other matters to which he has referred, I am in sympathy with the section of the Bill regarding the care and protection of our women.

speechtext:
Perhaps not every hon. member has a copy of the Criminal Code before him; therefore, in order to understand what we are doing, I will read the section as it now stands :
292. Every one is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to two years imprisonment and to be whipped who (a) indecently assaults any female; or, (b) does anything to any female by her consent which, but for such consent, would be an indecent assault, if such consent is obtained by false and fraudulent representations as to the nature and quality of the Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I may say in reply to my hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) that I am not able to answer his question on the spur of the moment. Before the committee rises I would like to add a word along the line of what my hon. friend from Grey (Mr. Sproule) has said. The Minister of Justice made a very emphatic and cogent argument against the whole principle of this Bill. The two principal points he made were, in the first place, that the infliction of this punishment for any offence is degrading and ought not to be imposed. In fact, if the argument of the Minister of Justice were carried to its legitimate conclusion, the enactments already upon the statute-book in that regard should be eliminated. The other point which the minister made is that it is impossible to carry out the punishment, that there is no person appointed by law upon whom that duty can be imposed, unless you are to presume that the warden of the penitentiary or the keeper of the jail can himself select one of his subordinates, and order him to perform what the minister regards as a degrading duty, degrading not only to the person who receives the punishment, but degrading to the person who inflicts it. Now the committee has arrived at the conclusion that in respect to one offence the punishment by whipping or flogging should be extended. Well, it seems to me that before this committee rises we ought to have some statement from the minister as to what the law is in that regard, and that this Bill should be amended so that the duty of carrying it out shall be imposed upon some definite official, who, if he fails to carry out the law, will himself be guilty of an offence. We ought not to put these punishments upon the statute-book and leave them to be disregarded, as they have been in the past, according to the testimony, not only of my hon. friend the Minister of Justice, but of gentlemen of the legal profession in this House who have given their experience.

I contend that I am in order. It has been argued that tenders are not properly opened, and that certain bad effects have resulted. I am endeavouring to prove that these bad effects have not resulted. Then I wish to show that what the hon. member for North Grey has stated, that owing to the manner in which tenders are opened it is impossible for Conservatives to obtain contracts from this government, is not a fact, and I am endeavouring to show that Conservatives have obtained and are obtaining contracts as the result of tenders they have put in to this government. I understand that Mr. Poupore has many times received contracts from this government as a result of tenders that he has put in under the method that is now in vogue.

I rise again to the question of order. I submit that the hon. gentleman has no right to discuss the tenders of Mr. Poupore or any one else under the ruling which you pronounced when this debate arose on a previous occasion.

I have already decided, on a point of order being taken, that the debate must be confined strictly to the motion and the amendment thereto, and anything irrelevant is out of order. I am not prepared to say that the last words were relevant not having heard them.

My argument and what I was stating was this: I understand that the motion before the House declares that the present method of opening tenders is not a good one, that evil results follow, and that in consequence some new method ought to prevail. In support of the resolution it has been stated that Conservatives do not tender for public contracts, and that men of all shades of politics belonging to all parties, ought to have fair play. I want to show that the argument is not a proper one, that the statements are not correct, and that it is not so that as a result of the present method of tendering Conservatives do not obtain fair play. In order to prove my contention I have been endeavouring to show and will show-and perhaps that is the reason why the point of order is so persistently urged-that Conservatives have obtained, do obtain and may obtain contracts from this government as other people do.

I venture to submit that this is no more relevant than was the consideration of the question regarding
dredging contracts in the harbour of St. John. If this is relevant then that is relevant.

Mr. Speaker, I might just call your attention to the fact that in this motion which is being discussed certain amendments to the regulations applying to the reception and opening of tenders were suggested by the mover to prevent any possibility of suspicion or tampering with tenders. Every gentleman on the other side of the House supporting this resolution, either directly or indirectly, stated his suspicion that there was tampering with tenders. Surely the hon. gentleman is permitted to answer that? Surely that is cognate to the question before the House? It is entirely different from the case of the Mayes dredging contract because that was clearly irrelevant, nobody having asserted that there was anything improner with respect to the reception or opening of those tenders.

Of course, my ruling is well-known to the House. Having decided that a certain matter is out of order it is no argument to say that it is in answer to what was said because a lot of what was said was irregular. I hope that hon. gentlemen will follow the rule and confine themselves to matters relevant to the question under discussion. Bourinot says that illustration is sometimes permitted, hut to undertake to discuss any specific case under this resolution would be clearly out of order.

I bow cheerfully and always to your ruling. I contend that I was doing what you say I am permitted to do- using this case as an illustration. I am prepared to show a long list of names but I am content to let that pass. I want to say in conclusion that it seems to me that it would tend very much to shorten the sessions of this House if members would confine themselves to charges which are not founded upon suspicion but which they can back up by evidence. The mover of the resolution suggests that there should be three persons present in place of two at the opening of tenders. Does he think that that would make any real change in the conditions or that if there is wrong-doing with two persons present there might not be equal wrong-doing with three? I do think there may be something in the suggestion of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Lake), who spoke a few days ago. He gave it not altogether as a suggestion but as a statement of the practice in some departments in Great Britain, and it was that the persons who are present when tenders are opened are changed from time to time, and that they are not always the same persons who are performing that duty. I think that the contention of my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works was well founded, and that there is a great deal in it

that if you say that contractors must be present when tenders are opened you simply lend yourself to a system that permits conniving and conspiring, and which will cause a great deal more evil and produce worse results than can or do exist to-day. The hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Middlebro) said:
I have always been in favour of the principle of letting contracts by public tender in a bona fide upright and conscientious manner.
No doubt the hon. member was sincere when he said that, and I should think every member of the House could use the very same words with an equal degree of sincerity. But the trouble with the hon. *gentleman (Mr. Middlebro) is that like too many of his friends on the other side he is prone to let his suspicion rather than his reason govern him. I believe that we should endeavour to adopt all methods that it is possible to adopt even if it were only for the purpose of lessening the suspicion of our friends on the other side of the House. If it were possible that the Auditor General or some such official in whom we all have confidence could be present when these tenders are opened, I would be agreeable to the adoption of such a system, but in the meantime I think the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) is the better of the two proposals before the House.

The amendment which has been presented by the hon. member (Mr. Guthrie) declares that the method of inviting, opening and considering tenders as embodied in the order in council of June 18, 1900, is in the opinion of this House a proper safeguard in the public interest. That order in council makes the following provision:
Where tenders are called for by any department of the government they shall be addressed to the officer of the department specified in the notice calling for tenders. In the notice it shall be specified that the tenders shall be under seal and endorsed 1 tender for	specifying the work or supplies for which tenders are called. When received they shall be stamped by the official to whom addressed, with the day and hour of their receipt, and placed under lock and key until such time as it shall be found convenient for opening them.
It does not seem to me that this provides any sufficient safeguard in the public interest. What is the meaning of the provision that the tenders shall be under seal? So far as I can understand, it only means that the person tendering shall affix his seal after his name, and it does not even go to the extent of providing that the tender shall be sealed up in a package or envelope. That may have been the intention of the gentleman who drafted the order in Mr. MILLER.
council, but he certainly did not say it. Therefore, there is absolutely no provision in the order in council as to tenders being inclosed in an envelope, and yet it is considered by the member for Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) a perfectly adequate safeguard. The other safeguard provided in this order in council is that the tender shall be placed under lock and key. That is the most absurdly slipshod expression I have ever heard of in an order in council or any other document, if the intention is to safeguard the public interest. In short, the order in council omits every single one of the very necessary safeguards which are contained in the resolution presented by my hon. friend from Grenville. The motion declares :
That in the opinion of this House tenders received in any department of government should be immediately placed in safe custody under seal so as to prevent any possibility or suspicion of tampering; and shall be opened in public at the time and place mentioned in the advertisement and in the presence of at least three principal officials of the department; and the persons so tendering or their duly authorized agents should be at liberty to attend at the said time and place and see such tenders opened and recorded, if they so desire.
When this motion was presented to the House last year, the right hon. the Prime Minister endorsed it in every particular except one, and that was with reference to the tenders being opened in public. But, even if you omit that provision, you will see that the order in council falls very far short of the motion of my hon. friend (Mr. J. D. Reid). Under the circumstances the attitude of the government in inviting the House to approve of a supposed safeguard which is not a safeguard at all, ought not to commend itself to our judgement. I believe that the provisions contained in the resolution of my hon. friend from Grenville are the provisions which will commend themselves to the people of this country as adequate and necessary safeguards in the public interest.

Some of the discussion on this resolution has been relevant, but a great deal of it has been irrelevant. I am as anxious as any other hon. gentleman in the House that a vote should be taken before six o'clock, and, therefore, I will prolong the debate for only a few moments. T purpose supporting the amendment of the hon. member for Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), and I will construe my vote as being an affirmation that the regulations now in torce are preferable to those proposed by the hon. member (Mr. J. D. Reid). I agree, to some extent, with the leader of the opposition when he says that the existing regulations * are not absolutely perfect; the drafting is

very imperfect indeed. The present regulations respecting the reception and opening of tenders for government work and supplies are, that they shall be stamped by the officials to whom they are addressed with the date and hour of receipt, and then placed under lock; that at a later date they shall be opened before the minister and an official of the department, and in the absence of the minister by another official of the department to be designated by him. The resolution of the member for Grenville proposes two changes only; first, that the tenders shall be opened in the presence of three officials, and, secondly, that the public as well as the tenderers shall have an opportunity of being present. Wherein are the present regulations defective, and if they are defective how can the suggestions contained in the resolution of the member for Grenville remedy the defect. I submit in all fairness that the recommendations contained in the resolution of my hon. friend (Mr. Reid) are not of a business like character and cannot commend themselves to anybody. To my mind it is utterly unimportant and trivial as to whether one or two or three or one hundred and three persons are present at the opening of the tenders. If there is any stage at vhich tenders should be protected it is while they are being received by the official of the department to whom they are addressed and while they are in his possession, and it is a mere waste of time to discuss how many persons shall be present when tenders are opened or whether the public shall be present or not. The resolution before the House does not suggest throwing around the officer who receives these tenders any protection or safeguard whatever.
Will not the fact of having them opened at the time and place mentioned in the advertisement do that ?

I shall come to that later. The hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) was right the other day when he said we must trust some one official in matters of this kind. As he said, the business of the world is carried on by reason of trust which man extends to his fellow men. Well, under the present regulations, and even under the regulations as proposed to be amended, the tenders would all be received by one official. If you do not trust this official what would you require to do in order to safeguard both public and private interests. You would require to have two or three men to watch this official as he opened his mail every morning, and two or three others keeping eye on the lock, and two or three more sleeping with this man at night, which might seriously disarrange domestic affairs. You would have to make sure that on the day and at the hour for closing tenders, the 19

time piece of this official was right, and perhaps you could not even trust the clock and a committee of two or three would have to go out and ascertain the time of day by the sun. My hon. friend from Qu'Appelle made a very good suggestion the other day. He suggested that if there be any objection to the mode of receiving and opening tenders, it is at this point the amendment should be made and not as regards how or when tenders should be opened, because that is after all, a very trifling matter which ought not to occupy the attention of the House one second. If you are going to make an amendment, I would say, let the officer who receives the tenders endorse on it the time and hour of reception and sign that with his own hand. Let him then pass the tender on to another officer, to be called the custodian of tenders, and let him also mark the time of reception as the former official. Then when the time for the reception has expired let these tenders be brought before the minister or his representative and be opened in the presence of the minister and these two officials.
As regards the proposition to have these tenders opened before the public, there is nothing in it to commend it to the judgment of this House. Just see what inconvenience that would occasion. But first let me say that the lowest tender is not always accepted. In some instances it may not be wise to accept it, either because of the financial inability of the tenderer or some other good reason. Imagine then what would follow if every person who tendered knew who were the other tenderers and what were their figures. One can easily understand how, when the lowest tender was rejected, the party who made that tender would storm the department in his attempt to satisfy the minister that he was quite competent and trustworthy and ought to get the contract. It is easy to understand how he would appeal to parliament and how hon. gentlemen opposite would make frenzied attacks on the government for not having accepted the lowest tender.
As to whether one or two or three are present at the opening of the tenders that is a matter which is utterly irrelevant and unimportant. But if you take these regulations as they stand, they are open to the construction that the tenders shall be opened in the presence of three officials. In this connection I desire to call the attention of the Minister of Public Works to what I think is imperfect drafting. The last clause reads: ' They shall be opened in the presence of the minister of the department calling for tenders and one of the principal officials of the department designated by that minister.' My reading of that clause up to that point is that the tenders are brought before the minister and one of his principal officers, and are opentd by the of-

fleer who received them, so that they are opened in the presence of three persons. True the remaining portion of the clause rather weakens my contention because it says: * Or in the presence of the minister or where it is not convenient for him to be present they shall be opened by two of the officials of the department to be designated by the minister.' It seems to me that there is a little confusion here which requires to be removed.
My hon. friend the mover of the resolution (Mr. Reid) laid special stress upon that part of it which provides for the opening of these tenders injrablic and in the presence of any of the tenderers who may see fit to attend. Of course if the tenders are opened in public it follows that the parties tendering may be present, but it would be very unfortunate if that feature were introduced into the regulations and it is one which ought not to commend itself to this House.

I quite agree, I simply want to emphasize one point in addition to those mentioned by the hon. leader of this side. The regulations provide that in the absence of the minister, he may name two officials who may open the tenders. The hon. Minister of Public Works in introducing these resolutions, told us the other day that that provision was inserted to meet cases in which the minister could not be present, and he cited Moncton where tenders are opened for hundreds of thousands of dollars and where it would not be convenient for the minister to be present.

At present there are no
tenders opened at Moncton.
I was not referring to what the Minister of Railways said, but to what the Minister of Public Works said, that they were opened at Moncton.
I do not want to interrupt, but I would not like that impression to go to the public, and I want the House to understand that tenders are not opened at Moncton.

I accept at once the statement of the Minister of Railways that the tenders are not opened at Moncton, but I do not know anything to prevent them being opened there. As a matter of fact, he says they are not, but they might be opened at Vancouver, or Victoria, or anywhere else in Canada. The regulations give the minister power to name two officials without stating who the officials shall be or their status. They may be two subordinate officials, and I submit that the provisions enabling the minister to name two subordinate officials anywhere in Canada would not command the confidence of the people in this country.

The first item is Commissioner and Chairman of Board of Customs. Last year the salary was $4,000 under the Act When he comes into class A of 1st division, it is $5,000. It is automatic. The assistant commissioner last year received $3,600, and the statutory increase will make it $3,700.

I thought the statutory increase was $50.

In the 1st division it is $100. The maximum of this salary is $4,000. Then, in the second division, subdivision: A, there are 13 salaries to be provided for. There were 8 before, and 5 were brought in from the outside. Before that there is the first division, subdivision B. That subdivision runs from $2,100 to $2,800. There are six estimated for in that, three that are permanent and three that were brought in from the outside. In the second division, subdivision A, which runs from $1,600 to $2,100, there are thirteen estimated for. Eight of these are in the inside service and five are brought from the outside. The next is second division, subdivision B. There are 121 estimated for, 104 of whom are brought in from the outside or were temporary. That class runs from $800 to $1,600.
You have made an increase of one? You had 104 outside, 16 inside and now you are providing for 121. Where does that extra one come in?
That is a position not yet filled. We are estimating for a typewriter that we will have to secure.
Will this typewriter be appointed by the commission?
Yes.

Is that the case with all officers? I had my attention drawn this afternoon to the question as to who would appoint the clerk of the committee on agriculture to succeed Mr. McLeod. Would that also come under the commissioners or would he be appointed by the officers of the House?

That is within the jurisdiction of this House, as I understand it. There are 23 in the third division, subdivision A, which runs from $900 to $1,200. Seven of these come from the outside. The third division, subdivision B, runs from $500 to $800. Five are brought in from the outside. Then, in the next class, that of the messengers, there are six estimated for. Five are brought in from the outside and there is an addition we are providing for. We will require another packer.

Will the minister just explain why it is necessary to have another packer. Is the work so much greater this year than last that it is necessary to have another? The feeling of the House is that the number of civil servants should not be increased but rather a reduction should be made. I hope the government will do what they can to keep d#\vn the expenditure and not make any more unnecessary appointments.

There is a great deal of work of that kind. All the different
*1)83

iports and outports have to have their stationery sent to them and the work of these packers consists largely in that. For some time we had an extra employee from the Department of Public Works doing that work, but we prefer to have an officer of our own. I agree with my hon. friend that it is desirable when our revenue is decreasing that we should go carefully. While we are providing for these appointments it does net mean absolutely that additional officers must be employed. I think the commissioner feels that it will be necessary to have this typewriter and this messenger, but if he finds he can get along without them the appointments will not be made.

The minister has indicated that the work of these messengers is largely in connection with sending out stationery to the ports and outports. Of course, the larger the number of outports the larger the number of messengers that will be required. I understand the government has given an assurance that there will be a customs port established at Milton, in my own county. I understand this because the gentleman who opposed me in the recent election gave the people there the assurance that there would be a customs port opened at that point. I suppose that this is one of the results of it. Evidently there is going to be an additional customs house and with that I am finding no fault. I would be very glad if the minister would open a custom house there. It is the county town and I do not know any reason why it should be without a customs port any more than any other county town in the province should be without one. Perhaps the minister can give us an assurance to-night as to whether he intends to implement the promise or not and if a port will be opened there. We had the very strongest assurances that a port would be opened in the interest of the people there. I take it for granted that the promise was given by the minister no matter who should be elected. I will not assume for a moment that the minister simply intended to open a customs house there if my opponent was elected because that would be a. kind of bribery held out to the electors that I do not believe the Minister of Customs would countenance. I believe that if he made the promise that a customs house would be opened in Milton it will be opened no matter who is elected. I have sufficient confidence in the minister to believe that he would not hold out a bribe to the people of that county or say that in the event of a supporter of the government being elected a customs house would be established. I am bound to believe he is too honourable a gentleman to offer a bribe of that kind to the electors. The people did not elect a supporter of the government, but nevertheless we expect Mr. PATERSON
that whatever promise was made in good faith by the minister, or the candidate who gave the assurance, will be carried out. It will be very useful to have a customs house at that place, and as the government has determined upon it I would like to have it as soon as possible. Perhaps the minister can inform the committee when it will he done?
When these estimates are through I am going to ask the committee to go on with the outside vote and then that question will come up.
You could answer that in a few minutes.

I suppose my hon. friend and myself are very much of the same mind. If there has to be a member of the Liberal persuasion from Brant, I suppose my hon. friend (Mr. Henderson) would as soon see me here as any one else. And on the other hand if there is to be a Conservative from Halton I am pleased it is the hon. gentleman. I do not claim any superior virtue, but I should not consider it proper for me to say in any county: If you will elect so and so you will get something, and if you don't you will not get it.

I would not have asked for this to-night if I thought the promise were only to be carried out in the event of the return of a supporter of the government. I do not believe the Minister of Customs would make any such one-sided pledge. Was the statement simply made by the hon. gentleman who opposed me to catch a few votes, or did the Minister of Customs make the pledge?
A great many requests come for these custom ports from members on both sides, and in the Northwest especially.
Answer the question straight. Did you make the promise?

No. I did not make the promise to Halton. I do not make any promise in connection with any of these requests. We say we will inquire whether the business will warrant it or not, and speaking now for Milton, I should judge it is a point that would deserve consideration if we find ourselves able to open any other port. If there has been a promise given, then because the election turned the way it did will not effect the question in any way.
Hear, hear.

It is reported in the press that Colonel Scott, collector of customs at Winnipeg, was about to be superannuated and a successor appointed. Would the Minister of Customs give me some information as to that?

I have been asked that question outside the House. So many statements get into the newspapers that are without foundation that one cannot keep track of them. All I can say is that so far as I am concerned, I have taken no steps in the direction of relieving Colonel Scott from the duties of his office. Colonel Scott has not asked to be relieved of his duties, and my personal inclination is that so long as an officer can discharge his duties properly and wishes to remain I do not view with favour a change being made. There has been no action taken on my part looking to the immediate retirement of Colonel Scott. I suppose Colonel Scott is now at an age that if he asked to be superannuated his request could be complied with under the superannuation Act. There has been no intimation on my part as to superannuating Colonel Scott against his will. Does that answer the question?
I think that answers it. Colonel Scott we know to be an energetic man who does not require superannuation, and of course the minister is speaking for the government.
I did not catch that.
The Minister of Customs has told us that Colonel Scott has not asked for superannuation, and I infer he will not be superannuated until he asks for it?
So far as I am aware he has not asked for superannuation, and of course if anything were to be done it would have to emanate from the Department of Customs.
Are we to understand that so long as Colonel Scott is able to perform his duties satisfactorily he will not be superannuated until he asks for it?

I have not had the question brought before me for action. I do not know how the report originated. What I have said is so long as the duties of an office are performed satisfactorily I would not be inclined to make a change unless, of course, the public interest would render it desirable.
Has there been any request for the superannuation of the collector of customs at Fredericton?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not like to interrupt hon. gentlemen, but I would point out that a discussion on the outside service has no relevancy to this vote for the inside service.
But the discussion has been allowed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is true, and I was about to suggest that it was not relative to this vote.
Will it not look bad in the eyes of the people that while the customs revenue is decreasing the government is adding to the number of officials?

It is for that reason that we are proceeding with great caution, but I think we are meeting the wishes of hon. gentlemen on both sides that there should be an increase in the salaries, and that the staff should be maintained at a strength sufficient to do the work. Although the amount received may not be so large there is still a great volume of correspondence to be attended to.

If we are going to open
new ports there might be some excuse, but the minister has not told us that new ports will be opened.

Would the minister
give the names of the 129 officials who were brought into the service during the last 12 months?

These were not all brought in during the last 12 months because many of them had been in the service for years. Some years ago we thought it desirable in the public interest that a number of statistical officers who formerly prepared statistics at outside points should be brought to head quarters at Ottawa so that the statistics would be gotten out at an earlier period and be of more use to the commercial community. These officers were brought to Ottawa about eight years ago, many of them had been in the service for years and years before that.
The hon. gentleman wants to know the names of the 129 who were brought in during the last 12 months.

The accountant gives me the following appointees during the year 1908:	F. Clemenson, appointed July
16, resigned September 15; R.' Braid, appointed March 26; J. Devlin, August 24; C. W. Dunlop, February 25; A. M. Dupuis, March 17; W. H. McElroy, March 7; F. H. Wood, June 17; Miss Sherry, July 17; T. A. Hastings, August 1; F. Barrette, February 5. The commissioner informs me these appointments were mostly made to fill vacancies.

I understand there are a number of officials engaged in compiling the Trade and Navigation returns and others engaged in preparing the returns of the Trade and Commerce Department, which are practically of the same nature. An arrangement might be made to have the figures for the two branches in the one publication and unnecessary expense saved.
The Trade and Commerce Department have no statistical officers and they use our tabulation.

The returns of the
Minister of Customs deal with imports entered for consumption and the Trade and Commerce returns give the imports whether entered for consumption or not. The returns prepared by the Department of Customs are most essential, but in the figures of the Trade and Commerce Department there is considerable duplication, which causes a great deal of expense and confusion as well.
