An item of this kind should not be allowed to pass without a protest from the members on this side, because the Minister of Customs has increased his staff by ten or twelve, which will entail a minimum increased expense of $8,000 a year, while at the same time the revenue is decreasing. I think the Minister of Customs is not conducting his department with that measure of economy which he would have us believe.
I think that the hon. gentleman did not understand me. They have not been increased by that number.
But there have been some ten new appointments in the face of a decreasing revenue.
They have been mostly to replace those who left the service.
Whom do they replace?

Mr. Dunlop replaces another who resigned. Mr. Dupuis replaced Mr. Wall, who went to the Post Office De-partement and Mr. Wood replaced another Mr. Wood, who resigned. Mr. Hastings succeeded Mr. Beilis, who was promoted.
Whom did Mr. McElroy replace?
He is a new appointment.
And Mr. Barrette?
He is also a new appointment.
And Miss Sherry?
That is another new appointment. Mr. Braid is a stenographer in the commissioner's office.
Then the hon. gentleman admits that at least six or seven thousand dollars are added to the expenditure of the department?
No, $800 is the highest salary.
And Mr. Devlin?
That was a new appointment in the statistical branch.
That makes about seven new appointments.
Five new appointments the accountant tells me. That is pretty economical out of a staff of one hundred and seventy-six.
With a decreasing revenue?

But we worked along all the time with an increasing revenue with a staff which we would have been justified in increasing. Last year was a year for revenue of which we never saw the like, and we are in hopes that this year there will be a renewed increase, a hope no doubt which my hon. friend shares.

If the hon. minister will read his speeches of two or three years ago when we had an increasing revenue, he will find that he justified the increase in his staff by the increase in the revenue. I have always been willing to admit that he was not so great a sinner as his colleagues, but I am afraid that, in face of the decreasing revenue of last year, he has shown that he is being led away by the bad example of his neighbours, and is increasing his staff in the face of a decreasing revenue.
In looking back at the speeches of other years, one forgets the circumstances at the time.

What right has the hon. gentleman to increase the number of employees in his department when there was not the same amount of work to be done? It looks as though he had just appointed some friends to fill positions which were made on purpose to accommodate them.

My hon. friend is a business man and he knows that we may have a decreasing revenue in a year when trade is depressed and yet have an increase in the work. There might be as many entries with a shrunken revenue as with a larger revenue. There would be as many invoices, or more, only they would be smaller in amount, and these would entail just as much work as in a year of greater revenue. We have not filled two of these places which became vacant, and I have not found the heads of my department at all extravagant.
The decrease in revenue rather affects the outside service, because the bulk of the customs work falls on the customs officers throughout the country.

But the statistical work deals with all of them. -Let me give another reason for the extra work. As the tariff existed prior to last year, certain material was allowed in free for certain purposes, and the importer would simply make a declaration that these articles were

for those purposes and they came in free. We found that the practice was abused and that goods brought in free for specific purposes had, in some cases, gone out of the hands of the importer into those of other men who were not entitled to this piivilege. I then changed the system and said that these articles, though free under the tariff, should pay the duty, and then the importers would file their claims for a rebate, which we would check by our officers. Hon. gentlemen can therefore understand how much work that cast on the department, but I believe that the department gained more in revenue than it cost by the extra expenditure.
The other evening it was admitted that some action should be taken to make civil servants work longer hours; and in view of the increases in their salaries they ought to work longer hours.
What does the hon. gentleman suggest as the number of hours they should work?
The feeling of the House was that the present hours were too short.
What hours would you suggest?
From nine to five would be suitable and reasonable, I think.
Not speaking of one de-partmtent more than another, but dealing with my own department alone, because it is now under discussion, I may say that our hours now are from nine to five.

If the hours of the other departments were increased, could not some clerks be transferred from those other departments to the customs ? Certainly it is not well to increase the staff with a decreasing revenue. The only possible justification, one would think, would be the expectation that the revenue is going to increase.
I am not passing judgment on the other departments. I give the hours that my department observe. We think that we get good work out of the officers.

Is it not well to consider all. this before we provide salaries for additional officers ? I have listened to gentlemen here who tell us that we have five or six hundred officials more than is necessary. If we are to add five more to the customs alone, it certainly does not look well. It seems most unfair to the people of the country to increase the staff while the revenue is decreasing.
know. I have given our hours, and I may say thq,t those are observed, for there is an attendance book. The minister does not have to sign it, but if he had, I think he would be found the only sinner. He does not attend very early, but perhaps makes it up in later hours.
The minister holds to the principle of increasing the staff with a falling revenue ?

No more than is necessary.
Department of Customs.-Contingencies, $9,000.

There is an increase here of $2,000 in sundries. This increase is only apparent, as the travelling expenses of officers at Ottawa whose travelling expenses, prior to September 1, 1908, were paid out of the vote for Board of Customs, in 1909-10, will be paid out of this vote for civil government contingencies. In 1907-8 the travelling expenses of these officers amounted to $1,673.95. Besides, there are the sundry expenses of the statistical office, $341, which will have to be paid out of contingencies.

I would draw the attention of the minister particularly to the argument used by himself a moment ago. I find the increase, over and above all that was paid to these members of the outside service to be over $1,600. To that add $150 per head for those who are brought in and those who are already in. And, in addition, there are the new appointments. Referring to the estimates of 1896, the total of employees in the inside service was 32. I find now that those in the inside service number 45, but the additions from outside make the total almost double what it was. In 1895, the expenditure was $36,800, whereas the expenditure now although it is impossible to distinguish between the two divisions, would be over twice the amount. Ten vacancies have occurred, but instead of trying to reduce the staff, the minister has filled the vacancies and appointed new officers besides. The minister's argument at one time was that the staff must be increased because the revenue was going up, but now that the revenue is going down there is no decrease in the staff. Now the same hon. gentleman argues that a diminution of the revenue brings about no decrease in the necessary work. If this can be justified, surely the revenue is no guide to the expenditure of this government.
Going back to 1896, you find a different position altogether.

We had an
economical government then.

As I say, I am not Mr. PATERSON. I do not want to say passing judgment on other departments, anything against my predecessors. I think Work in others may be heavier for all I I that the gentlemen that you have had at

the head of this department were pretty close-I do not know but that, perhaps, they were as close as I am. But look at the comparison of revenue; nineteen millions in 1895, last year fifty-eight millions-three times the amount. We are going to drop eleven or twelve millions this year, but I expect we are going to pick up next year and these are the estimates for next year. I am sure that all hon. gentlemen will join with me in the hope that the revenue will increase. Since 1896 the revenue has increased threefold. I do not think the number of entries increased that much, but still there was a vast increase in the number of entries. An entry of $10 takes as long to make as an entry of $1,000.

I am not able to follow the hon. minister's logic. When asked for an explanation for that increase in the number of his staff by 5 clerks, he told us that with a decreasing revenue there was as much work as, when there was an increasing revenue. That might be a reasonable answer for retaining the same number on the staff, but it is not an answer for increasing the staff by 5 clerks. Then, in explaining the expenses on sundries, he proposes to increase the allowance by nearly 50 per cent. We who are from the rural parts of the country and not acquainted with handling millions, would like to know all about these sundries. We know that sundries, like charity, often cover a multitude of sins. I would like the minister to explain not only the expenditure of $1,500 or $1,600, but to explain to us new members from the country the whole sum of the sundries.
I am from a rural county like the hon. gentleman himself. This sum of money was paid last year for the same service, travelling expenses of officers that were in the outside service.
Generally, what are the sundries for?

If the hon. gentleman will look at the Auditor General's Report, page F-5 he will see the customs contingencies all set out.
Salaries and contingent expenses of the several ports in the Dominion including pay for overtime of officers, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, $1,800,000.
There is an increase here of $95,000.

Can the minister tell us how much of this $95,000 increase is due to overtime earned by officers? I should think that when these officers work only four and a half hours a day we should not have so much overtime.

At centres such as Halifax, St. John, Montreal, Hamilton and other places trains are coming in at all Mr. PATERSON.
hours of the night and you have to have officers there to attend to them. In Montreal a steamer comes in; she unloads day and night and you have to have your officers there to attend to that. The hours of these officers are from 8 to 6 and in the olden times they got no overtime. When they worked overtime we used to make the railway and steamboat companies pay them. The companies came to my predecessor as well as to myself and reported that they saw no. reason why they should do that. They said that the revenue of Canada should be looked after by officers in the pay of Canada and, with a disinclination to swell the expenditure of my department for some years, I took the position of my predecessors and waved them off. Finally their argument prevailed with me. I could not see any reason why a. railway or a steamboat company should have to pay officers of the Dominion government. It was our duty to look after the Dominion revenue. I might have said: Do not run your trains at night; do not come into the harbour at night, and if I had said so they would have been forced to pay the officers. We assumed that burden ourselves, and now these men who were largely paid in days gone by by the transportation companies are paid by ourselves, except that if they want any Sunday labour we will not give it to them. We give it to them on holidays, but on Sundays we do not. With officers working during the day the question might arise as to whether a man having worked from 8 to 6 o'clock is in a position to do two or three hours more labour, but unfortunately in many cases the pay of our officers at these large ports is such that it is impossible almost for some of them to live on what they get, and there is a very great desire on their part to augment the salaries which they earn between eight and six by putting in two or three hours at night and getting 25 cents an hour for it. The question has occurred:	Would it be better for us to engage men specifically who should go on at six o'clock at night and remain until six o'clock next morning to do the work that is now done or allow these men to have a few hours extra work, which work arguments their salaries and which, they .claim, does not give them more than they require to provide a living for themselves and their families. That is the whole explanation.
Can the hon. gentleman tell us approximately the amount that is given for overtime? Is it not a fact that there are some who are employed for night work?
It says ' including overtime.'
These items will be chargeable other years as well as this year. That does not account for the increase.

I do not know anything as to that, but the hon. gentleman asked a specific question and I was answering that. What we w'ant to do with this vote is to provide that in case we have to open some new ports we may be able to do so. We are fighting shy of that as far as we can. We have so many applications.
Are there any new employees to pay out of this amount?

Yes, there will be new employees. But we have to estimate that we may, notwithstanding our disinclination to increase the number of ports, find cases that are of such merit that we will have to yield. We want to do as well as we can this year and we want to do as as little as possible in the way of supplementing salaries, though, if our feelings were consulted, we would do a great deal more. With the decline in our revenue we will have to ask the officers to be patient with us, more especially as within the last two or three years in the Customs Department there have been increases of salaries to outside officers of between $200,000 and $300,000. While that seems a large sum of money, but when you spread it from the Atlantic to the Pacific with nearly 2,000 employees, you can see that it would not be a very large increase for any one. There are some who have complained to us that in our division of the money their cases have been overlooked. We do not intend to give it to every one, but there are some cases in which they say that an injustice has been done to them. We propose to ask for a few thousand dollars so that if there are some cases of exceptional merit which have been overlooked we may be able to deal with them, and, if there are new ports to be opened, that we may have the money to open them. There are new towns constantly developing in the Northwest which to-day may not be of much importance, but which within the next twelve months may have to be established as customs ports.

I believe that the outside service is underpaid in many instances and I congratulate the Minister of Customs that he has decided to increase the salaries of his officials in the outside service. I believe that will meet with the commendation of the House. Is the minister giving the increases on account of merit or simply as a percentage on the present salaries?

We have endeavoured to consult with the collectors at the large ports and we have taken the reports of our inspectors at the smaller ports in making these increases. Three years ago there were to be found men in Montreal who had been fifteen or twenty years in the custom service and who only received $500 a year. We were able to increase their salaries first to $550, then to $600, and then to $650. My aim is that in the large cities where living is expensive, every officer shall have at least $700 a year. They work faithfully from eight o'clock until six, and I think the Dominion of Canada will not want them to work for less than $700 a year. If I get this money I will consider some of these cases. I say frankly and fairly that no consideration guided the department in the distribution of this money which could be considered an unworthy reason. I know of course from the date Of their appointment how they came into the service but I can say that simply because they did not come in under me, no officer was debarred from that which was his fair due. You will have to trust us in the distribution of this money to do what we think is right and fair to the various officers. If any hon. gentleman knows of any case where merit has not been recognized and if he lets me know I will be very pleased to consider it.

In view of the invitation given to us by the minister I wish to mention a very peculiar condition of things in connection with the custom office in the city of Rossland. In the early days of Rossland we had a large custom business there, but with the collapse of the boom the number of entries and the custom business generally decreased very materially, so that there was not employment for one half of the former staff. Mr. B. R. Macdonald who was Collector of Customs at Rossland, and who I do not hesitate to say is one of the very best officers in the whole service, applied to be removed to Prince Rupert, believing that would become an important place and that his long and faithful service justified promotion. He was sent to Prince Rupert but was not appointed collector. Things drifted along at Rossland for some time, and the remaining officials in the office were sufficient to carry out the work, but eventually the collectorship was declared vacant. There was in the office at Rossland a man who had been in the service for seventeen years or more and who had been collector, but no sooner was the collector-ship declared vacant than the Liberal Association called a meeting to receive applications for the position and they recom-

mended a certain man who not only had absolutely no experience in custom work but who had never done clerical work of any kind in his life. He was a blacksmith. I am not reflecting on his occupation in any way. I respect the man very much and he was a clever man in his own business, but he had no experience in clerical work and yet because he had been an influential party worker he was, on the recommendation of the Liberal Association, placed in the position at $1,600 a year, over the head of a man who had been in the service for seventeen years. Now, here is a case in which merit has been overlooked^ Here was a man taken from a blacksmith shop and given a salary of $1,600 a year while the two other men in the Rossland custom house who had served for years received $900 a year and $1,200 a year respectively All the new collector at Ross-land had to do was to go to the office each day and one of the regular officials who was well versed in the law, and who was now made subordinate to him, had to instruct him in his duties. For this sinecure, as I say, he is receiving $1,600 a year. No wonder there is an increase of $95,000 in this vote. Now, there is more in the story. When Mr. Macdonald went to Prince Rupert, although he was one of the best men in the service, he was refused the appointment of collector and a man who had never been in the customs service and who had no experience whatever was appointed to the position. Strange to say when the new political appointee to the collectorship found that the boom did not come at Prince Rupert as he expected he believed he could make more money back in the city of Vancouver and he resigned. These are too glorious instances to show how the money of the people is wasted. Why does this collector at Rossland receive $1,600 a year practically for a sinecure? The other men were doing the work and doing it well, and I venture to say that there is a continued falling off in the revenues of the office; so that there was absolutely no need for the appointment. And why did not the men who had long worked in the service of the country receive that advance which the minister says he gives to those in the inside service? Why should not the outside service be treated in the same way as the inside? The hon. minister assured us that when a vacancy occurs in the inside service the other men are moved up but he has not carried out that principle in the outside service. It is appointments made in this way which destroy confidence in the government of this country. I would like an explanation of the instances I have referred to.

The hon. gentleman is no doubt stating that he thinks it his duty to point out to this House, but I do not think he knows all the circumstances. My Mr. GOODEVE.
recollection is that Mr. MacDonald, who was collector at Rossland, asked to be transferred to Prince Rupert on the ground of ill health and his request was granted.
He was collector at Rossland, and he asked for a similar position at Prince Rupert, but another man was made collector there and Mr. Macdonald was made subordinate to him.

But he is there and is in receipt of his salary. As we presumed, Mr. Macdonald was going to remain at Prince Rupert and another collector had to be appointed instead of giving the appointment to Mr. Grigor there was another person recommended, and I hope he is a good officer. If the hon. gentleman says he is not, I shall have to get reports on him from my inspector. I may be asked why the position was not given to Mr. Grigor. I am informed that he has to do relieving duties at times, because in a province like British Columbia, we require to have at these different ports an extra man to take the place temporarily of an officer at another port who may be ill. If there has been any injustice done, I shall be very sorry, lout I do not think I am open to the charges of extravagance. My hon. friend will not say we should discharge an officer at any port simply because there may be a falling off in the revenue.

What I complain of is that they took an outside man of no experience and unnecessarily placed him in office in view of the decreasing revenue and entries. They did so purely for political purposes. I was not referring to Mr. Grigor, whom the hon. Minister has mentioned. Mr. Grigor is a good man and a friend of mine, but during my election he deliberately left his office and went to Nelson and stayed two weeks there electioneering against me while all the time he was drawing his salary. I am not saying any thing against him because he has had experience in the office and is a personal friend of mine, but what I object to is that out of that increased vote of $95,000, I can point to two instances where the money of the country is paid to men who are appointed simply because offices had to be made for them.
But there was a vacancy was there not ?

When the revenue and the entries were falling off, the office could have been left vacant. When one man could fill it for five or seven months without any assistance what necessity was there for making another appointment. I am not asking the minister to discharge anybody because it would be most unfair to discharge an employee on the ground that there was a temporary falling off in the

revenue; but when an office became vacant and there was no need to fill it, why appoint a man to that office, especially one who has no experience. In that one instance you could have saved $1,600. I am not reflecting upon your appointee further than to say that the office should have been given to the man who had done good and faithful service during 17 years.
It would not do to leave a port without a collector.
Why not give the place to the man who deserved promotion ?

The thing has been done and if it be wrong we will have to look into it. But you could not leave the port without a collector. The vacancy was caused by the collector asking to be removed to Prince Rupert. We went on for a time with the officer in charge and then another officer was appointed temporarily to do the work. I suppose that Mr. Stephens was not able to attend to all the work.

There are three employees in that office. I am not divulging anything of a private character because it was published in the Daily ' Press ' that the Liberals had called a meeting for the express purpose of recommending a man for the appointment. There were three or four applicants, and among them were men who had been long in the service and were, entitled to promotion. The government passed over a man who had done faithful service for 17 years and who still has his old salary of $1,200 and they placed a political partisan over his head in the office at $1,600.
Will the minister take note of the facts that this customs officer whom he appointed at $1,600 a year engaged in political work ?
I was very sorry to hear that.

Will the minister dismiss this officer, according to the resolution of the House for which he voted, that civil servants must not take any part in elections? It is charged that one of his officers vacated his position and went out on the stump for two weeks at a time, in aid of the Liberal candidate.

I trust the hon.gentleman is mistaken. If the hon. gentleman will write me a letter stating that this officer neglected his duty and spent his time electioneering against him, I will write to the officer and ask him what explanation he has to make, as I think it is always fair to the officer to do.
The hon. gentleman made the statement from his seat in the House.

I am not making a charge against the officer but against the minister and his department for making an appointment for political purposes. We have two excellent men there; Mr. McDonald is one of the best men in the service, and I have no charge to make. But I am asked to vote tor an increase ot $95,000, the revenue is falling off, and here is a case where an unnecessary officer is appointed.

I think it was proper to fill the office and I have never yet, I frankly confess, considered the fact of a man being a Liberal as a bar to his appointment to office, other things being equal; that is not done under party government.

Does this vote contemplate an increase in the staff?
' Mr. PATERSON. Yes.
How large?

I cannot tell you that, it will depend on the requirements. Of course in a country developing as rapidly as Canada is we cannot estimate exactly what increases will be required in the Customs service 14 months ahead.
Does that include the port about which the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) inquired, Milton?
There is one of the points we have to consider.
Is that estimated for?
We have not worked out any detailed scheme as yet.

The hon. member for Kootenay (Mr. Goodeve) has brought up an interesting question as to the principle followed by the minister and his department in making appointments in the Customs service. We are told that in the inside service men are appointed according to merit and service; is the same principle followed in the outside service? Are appointments made by the promotion of efficient officers to vacancies or are they made by an outside political pull or by the award of a patronage committee?
Promotion does not follow in the outside service as a matter of course. As a rule if a collectorship at a port becomes vacant a new appointment is made.
There have been promotions, but it is not the rule.
Yes, there have been promotions, but that is not the rule.

Does not the minister think it a better policy to promote a man who has done efficient service rather than appoint a

new man? At Port Colborne a vacancy was caused by the death of Mr. Sidey, but I notice a new man has been appointed, and the local paper states that although he is the son of a worthy citizen of Welland, he has been for a number of years living in Chicago. In such a case, where there are good officers, they should have been promoted.
I think there is only the one official there.
There were two, Mr. Rams-den the landing waiter, and the late Mr. Sidey.
Mr. Ramsden held a dual position, partly under the Customs and partly under the Railway Department.

The answers given by the minister have been most satisfactory to me. I understand this item deals with the outside officers. There has been a good deal of talk here about the salaries and hours of the inside service. I have always believed that the inside service has been starved, and I am pleased to see that their salaries have been increased. Is there any indication of increase in the salaries of the outside service? Are the salaries provided by this item the same as have been in force for some years? because I have the same feeling towards the outside service. It, too, is being starved. The cost of living has increased greatly in the last few years. I hope the minister has that feature in view.

This year we granted increases to officers in the different provinces as follows:	Number of	AggregateProvince.	increases.	amount.Ontario	310	$23,430Quebec	274	14,400New Brunswick	55	3,100Prince Edward Island.	13	800Nova Scotia	121	6,600Manitoba	52	3,650Alberta	14	1,200Saskatchewan	13	1.050British Columbia.. ..	63	5,150
These are the increases granted during the past year. The hon. gentleman will see that this is a small increase among so many officers. Many of the increases have been only $50 or $100 or $150, but the hon. gentleman can readily see that even with the increased amount granted each year for three or four years past by parliament the increases have not been large. But when you spread it over about two thousand officers from the Atlantic to the Pacific it gets pretty thin.

If it is convenient for the minister to give it, I would like to get some information. Take the case of a customs port with a revenue of $200,000 a year, what is the salary paid to the chief Mr. LALOR.
officer there? I want to make a comparison between the salary of a first-class clerk in the inside service and that of an officer in charge of a port such as I speak of, and distant, perhaps, two thousand miles from Ottawa. If I can get the information, I believe I can show that such an officer is not properly paid.

There is a little difference in the provinces, but in such a case as the hon. gentleman speaks of, the salary of the collector would be from $1,500 to $1,800. Of course, there are other officers at the port.
Does not the minister sympathize with the idea that these men should be paid more?-for I believe they should.

I can certainly ask for more if the House will give it to me. Personally, it will be very pleasing for me to do so. But I have asked all I can venture to ask, and even when I ask for the amount I do, there seems to be a disposition to criticise me very closely.

I do not believe there is a business in this country in which men having the custody of $200,000 a year are paid only $1,500. I have no desire to embarrass the hon. minister, and am satisfied with the answers he has given. Some gentlemen here do not appear to be satisfied with the conduct of affairs in British Columbia, but I would remind them that they are overlooking that doctrine 'To the victors belong the spoils'-a doctrine which has been developed as a hot house- plant, but this, however, is not the time to discuss that.

I do not want to vote money until I have some idea what is going to be done with it. As junior member for Halifax, one of the leading customs ports of Canada, I desire to say that, if it were not for the overtime that the officers there work, they would starve-a man has to work night and day for a mere existence. We have from 67 to 70 men there working at salaries of from $650 to $750. The collector is a man who left a very lucrative business to take his present position, a man held in the highest esteem by the citizens of Halifax. He receives $3,200 a year. I am not complaining of what is paid to the inside service, but you pay a first-class clerk on the inside service more than you pay our collector. If it were not for the honesty of the people of Halifax and Nova Scotia, we would not get as much revenue as we do. If these officers were not honest men, they would pay themselves. The minimum, the very lowest, salary that an officer should be asked to work for in a port like Halifax should be $1,000 a year, and it should run from that to $4,000 for the collector. Next to the collector comes the surveyor, who

now receives a salary of $1,500. Then we have two chief clerks getting only $1,200 a year, then the cashier at $1,150. And there are from 10 to 15 who run from $1,000 down, with about 70, as I have said, with between $650 to $750. I do not think that we should have more officers, but we should try to pay the officers we have fair salaries. If the minister will give me some reason to believe that the money he asks for is going to be used to augment the salaries of these men, so that they can make a decent living for their families, I am prepared to support this item. Perhaps the other cities are in the same position, but I do not think their position can be quite as bad in this respect as that of Halifax. If the Minister of Customs can say that he will look after Halifax, and that the minimum salary of a customs officer in Halifax shall be $1,000, that will do, and I shall feel that there is a desire on the part of the Customs Department to treat the cities outside of Ottawa fairly. I am not saying a word against the inside service or the gentlemen who occupy positions in it, but while Halifax is a pleasanter place to live in, it is as dear as Ottawa. I want to see our men get something like a fair share of the money we vote for the department. If the minister will assure me that he is going to deal with those officers of whom I have spoken-and he knows the collector of Halifax and the officers there, and I am sure he will agree that they are, as I have said, a fine lot of men; I will say no more.

Unhappy is the lot of a Minister of Customs, with some critics asking him to increase his estimates tenfold and others declaring that he is already asking an unreasonable amount. I admit that our officers i,n Halifax are good, they work hard, and I suppose living has increased in Halifax as it has in other places. But when you ask me to bring them up to $1,000, I would have to come to parliament and ask for over half a million of money, and I do not think parliament would be disposed to do that. Last year, for instance, the increases amounted to $59,450, that was distributed over all the provinces. Here I am only asking for one-tenth of what the hon. gentleman asks me to do. Within the last few years we have made increases running into the hundreds of thousands. While I am proposing $60,000 to increase certain salaries, I am bringing upon myself a mass of communications and representations, and raising hopes from the Atlantic to the Pacific that I shall not be able to gratify, because there will not be a man in the service, scarcely, who would not wish to get a share. We will pick out what we consider the most deserving cases. Every officer in the Dominion will think he is entitled to a piece of it.

I think we ought to be fair to the minister. I think he is perfectly right in asking for this increase. I understand he will not use it unless it is necessary. We must'remember that this country is growing, and there will likely be new offices opened. While we are criticising the expenditures we must be fair. In my own town, for instance, we have a very good officer who is getting, I think, only $700 or $750 a year. If the revenue went down one-half, are you going to close that office ? That man cannot work for less than that, and it is not fair to ask him to do it. I am in sympathy with this estimate the minister is asking for. Any person can see that it is necessary to provide for the future. There is another thing. It is impossible for the minister or any other minister to make appointments that will please everybody. I understand that these appointments are made on the recommendation of the local executive of the Liberal party. If there is an appointment made in Rossland, as has been explained here to-night, I fancy the minister is governed by the reports from the executive, and I fancy that if we were in power, in making appointments, the advice of our local representative would receive earnest consideration. I can understand, as the minister says, that he does not know whether there will be one more or a dozen more officers required next year.

I notice here the ever recurring phrase 'Notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act to the contrary.' I understand when we amended the Civil Service Act that one of the purposes was to do away with that very thing.
The new Act does not apply to the outside service.
You are dealing with the outside service now.
We are working under the old Act, and I had to put in these words, because otherwise we could not pay for overtime.
The minister explained a few minutes ago that part of this increase was required to enable the customs to pay the officers for their overtime work.
That has been done for several years.

I understood that the system in vogue for several years was that when officers went to the railway stations after hours, they collected from the railway for their overtime. I have understood since that instead of allowing the officers to collect from the railway the government collects from the railway and divides that among the officers. I wanted to know if that is the case. In my own town, for example, for years and years the officers

would go down to the Canadian Pacific Railway, perhaps at 9 or 10 at night, and for their overtime they would send in a bill at the end of the month for $40 or $50 as the case might be, and the Canadian Pacific Railway would pay it. Now has the Canadian Pacific Railway been relieved of that expense, do the government pay it now and collect nothing from the railway, or does the government collect from the railway and divide it among the employees?

No. In the old times, as I have explained, we required the transportation companies to pay for this overtime. But they never paid the officers direct, we did not permit that. The government collected from the company the amount of the overtime of the men and paid it to the men. The railway companies did not pay the officers direct. But a few years ago, when parliament sanctioned the change I asked for, we relieved all the transportation companies of this payment of overtime, and it is now paid out of the Dominion treasury. We require the transportation companies to pay now only in exceptional circumstances. For Sunday labour we will not pay, but we make them pay to us, and we divide it up among the men.
In the city of Halifax is it not a fact that the merchants pay the extra time of the officers ?

I s*ppose this is what the hon. gentleman refers to. Importers bringing goods into the county are supposed to deal on a cash basis. We do not let them have their goods until we get their money, that is a safe way of doing business. But as there are large importations made by merchants who do not want to pay all the money at once, there has been known for years what we call the bonding system; that is, we have a bonded warehouse in which they may store their packages of dutiable articles. They do not want to pay the duty all at once, which may amount to a very large sum, and they put their packages into a bonded warehouse and take them out as they wish, five or ten packages at a time. They apply to us, and we send one of our officers to open that warehouse and deliver to them the number of packages they want, and collect the duty thereon. For many years we charged a uniform rate of $40 for a bonded warehouse. One man might put $300,000 worth of goods in a bonded warehouse, and another only $50,000 worth, perhaps another $10,000, but none of them would pay more than $40. In the case of a large importer we found that it would take perhaps the whole time of one of our lockers to attend to that one house, while another man who paid as much for his store house, $40, might only require the service of a locker once or twice Mr. J. D. REID.
a week. We thought that was not fair. We said: We will make the men pay us who have bonded warehouses, it is a privilege given to them, they are saving the interest on the duty which is a large amount and if they are going to take the time of our officers for their own convenience and benefit we will establish a uniform rate that they shall pay for the time that they use our officers.
Surely the Minister of Customs does not mean to tell us that about the ordinary bonding system in the customs.
That is the only way that the merchant pays anything and that is what the hon. gentleman is asking about.

I think there is another way. I think the Minister of Customs has given a wrong impression of the bonded system. He has given the impression that a man puts his goods into the bonded warehouse because he wants to save his money. Does the minister mean to tell us that there are not hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of goods put into the bonded warehouse and then ship-ed out to another country?
Yes.
Well, then, how are they saving money in that case?
How did they get the goods there? Do you suppose that we leave the doors open to them to go and put the goods in without an officer being there?
That is where you get your revenue.
If they do not have the services of the officer they do not pay him.

Oh, that is not the matter I am discussing. Did the minister not say distinctly that the reason for the bonded warehouse was that a man could put his goods in there and save his money because he would not have to pay the duty until he took them out? I am sure that 25 per cent of the goods go out of the bonded warehouse in Halifax without paying duty at all, and the deputy minister of Customs knows that. I do not want the impression to go abroad that the merchants in Halifax put their goods into the bonded warehouse for the purpose of saving money when they do not.
Carried.
I beg your pardon. I am not carried yet. Is it not a fact that the merchants pay for the overtime of the officers after hours? There may have been a change made but if so it has been made recently.
I am very sorry if I have offended the hon. gentleman in any way by my allusion to the fact in my explanation that the bonded warehouse means a saving to the merchants storing their goods there.
I would like to ask the hon. gentleman if I am not right in my statement about the warehouse?
1 am going to answer the hon. gentleman.
Well I want an answer, yes or no. If I am right I am right, and if I am not, I am not.

I said they put their goods in there for the purpose of saving revenue. Let me put it in a happier way and say that by virtue of putting their goods in there they save it, and I do not think it is any disgrace to a man to do it and I see no cause for offence. If these goods are going to be re-exported they cannot go into the .bonded warehouse unless our officer is there to see them go in and they cannot take them out a month or a year after unless our officer is there to see the goods as they go out. For the services the officer renders they pay and they pay nothing else.
Is not that officer paid his regular salary from the vote we give every year?
He is paid his regular salary, but do not confuse this with overtime. The officer doing this does not get the money paid for the bonded warehouse. It comes into the Dominion Treasury.
Has the minister any idea what amount was collected for the services of lockers last year?

Does the minister not think that the government, having relieved the railways of a similar charge, it would be a proper thing to relieve the commercial community also? Are the railways and steamboat companies more deserving a consideration in the monetary sense than the mercantile community? That is a question I would like the minister to consider during the coming year. It is not so much the amount of money that.they are required to pay for the services of an officer as the difficulty of getting an officer when he is wanted.

It is an advantage to a man to be able to defer the payment of duties and especially when it runs into thousands or tens of thousands, or, as in some cases, hundreds of thousands of dol lars. But he is one man perhaps in a business community of a hundred of fifty who gets that advantage. Should the other men who do not avail themselves of it, and
who get no benefit from it, contribute towards that expense or should we not get that $29,000 for the service rendered to the man who has the benefit of it and place that money in the Dominion Treasury? Outside of the question of overtime, the money comes into our treasury. The principle is that the man who gets the benefit pays for it, while the man who does not take advantage of it pays nothing for it. I am sure that the merchants using the bonded warehouses will admit that it is absolutely fair.
The minister has not answered my question. I asked him if there was not money paid by merchants and shipping men at Halifax for extra time. I would like to get that question answered, yes or no.

I am told that there have been $101 paid by all the bonded' houses for overtime throughout the Domino11 of Canada, and that has only been when they wanted an officer before eight in the morning or after six o'clock at night.
Mr. CROSBY Can I get the minister to leave bonded warehouses for two or three minutes and tell me if there has been any money paid to tide waiters and officers on ships which come into Halifax to discharge cargo by steamship agents and shipping men?
For Sundays.
And for no other time?
No other time, the^case?^*^ How long has that been
About three years.
I thought it had taken place very recently. 1 would like to know when they were relieved.
That is a reform we have made.
A reform! Then, I want you to make another reform and give the men the money you have taken away from them. If you will give them the same proportion I am prepared to vote for these estimates.

If they have the services of this officer between eight in the morning and six at night, according to the hours they use him for their own benefit, they must pay us, the money goes into the Dominion Treasury and it is not given to the officer, but if they take an officer before eight in the morning or after six at night they pay us that money, which money we pay to the officer and which has amounted for the whole Dominion of Canada to $101.
Is it the intention to superannuate the inspector of customs at Fredericton?
It is proposed to superannuate the collector at Fredericton.
Has the minister any objection to state what applications he has received for the office, and from whom?
I am safe in saying we have received no applications yet and I do not know that I am anxious to get them. The superannuation has not been passed and we are not yet in a position to fill the office.

Does the Minister of Customs purpose making the further reform of providing out of the consolidated revenue fund a sufficient sum to pay the cost of advertising the meetings of these political committees who recommend appointees. Would not that be a logical addition to the expenditure of the country?
I have not had an opportunity of studying how this was done in times past but I will look into it.

The minister has not only looked into it but he has acted upon it in the case of Rossland. In view of the expose in that case I should think the minister ought to pay the extra salary of $1,600 out of his own pocket.
Did the collector at Fredericton apply for superannuation?
I am not aware that he did.

I understood the minister to say when speaking of Winnipeg that there would be no superannuation except upon the application of the collector himself. Why is that rule departed from in the case of Fredericton?

I qualified that statement by saying that the collector should be able to discharge the duties of the office. The public interest may require the superannuation of a collector without his applying for it.

From whom has the minister received any information that the collector at Fredericton is not capable of performing the duties of the office? That statement of the minister will be a surprise to the people of Fredericton.
We judged from the inspector's report, that it was advisable this step should be taken.
And without any application for superannuation being received from the collector himself.
Yes.
When does the minister ^propose to superannuate the collector at Fredericton?

It is in process. These superannuations have to pass the Treasury Board who inquire into the merits. You can superannuate an official for cause after he attains 60 years of age, but the Treasury Board do not approve superannuating a man simply because he is 60 years old unless it is for the benefit of the service.
The benefit of the party.
Oh no.
Is this action taken upon the report of any person?
The report of our inspector.
Would the minister bring that down?

I don't think it would be well to ask for that. The inspector reports to us confidentially in a measure, and to publish the report might hurt somebody's feelings. I have no objection to bring it down, but I would rather show it to my honourable friend. Of course I do not impute anything wrong but it was considered advisable to superannuate the collector in this case.

I believe that the minimum salary of customs officials in the city of Halifax should be $1,000. I believe also that they should be brought under the Civil Service Act because there is always a tendency for the man with a pull to get more than others who have not the pull, and I know very good officers in Halifax who have not had an increase of salary for several years. The only way they can get fair treatment is to bring them under the Civil Service Act. If the minister would indicate there would be a general increase in the salaries of the Halifax officials, I would be satisfied..
Salaries and travelling expenses of inspectors of ports and of other officers on inspection and preventive service, including salaries and expenses in connection with the board of customs and salary of chief and general inspector at $4,000 per year, $135,000.
There is a reduction of $104,500 in this vote caused by the transfer to the inside service of officers whose salaries were formerly charged to the vote for the outside service.
Was there any particular group of officers so transferred?
It would principally refer to the clerks in the statistical office,
Were there any new officials appointed in 1908 under this item?

They would be included in the names I have given. I have given the names of the new employees of my department.

Miscellaneous-Printing and stationery subscriptions to commercial papers, flags, dating stamps, locks, instruments, etc., for various ports of entry, express charges on samples, stationery and forms, legal expenses, premiums on guarantee bonds and uniforms for customs officers, $87,500.

Will the minister refer to page F-42 of the Auditor General's Report? He will there find an item of $827 paid W. G. Charleson-a name that comes up frequently in our public accounts-for a lot of goods. Were these goods purchased by tender? I find an item of 24J dozen of padlocks amounting to $250.50, or equal to $10.33 a dozen.

These are all purchases made at different times during the year and tenders are not asked. The locks are for bonded warehouses, and have to be a special kind of padlock, which cannot be opened by the ordinary key. The purchasing officer is one who has been in the department for 30 years and in whom we have full confidence, and he has certified to the price as reasonable.
I suppose the minister has a patronage list the same as the other departments?
Oh, very little.

We find in all these items the same names cropping up as appears in the patronage list of the other departments. The hon. gentleman takes the ground that becauses he has the certificate of his purchasing officer the prices are reasonable. Well, when we complained of the excessive prices in the Public Accounts Committee last year we had the minister pleading that it was an outrage to insinuate that any of their officials would certify to prices which were not absolutely correct. The result of the investigation, however, made by the commission appointed by the government themselves has proved that such certificates are not at all to be relied on, and this man Charleson is one of those who charged prices much higher than are charged private individuals for the same goods. Although the Minister of Customs does not require to purchase as many supplies as some of the other ministers, he is just as guilty as the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur) who is smiling now over the way in which he administered his department, and which enabled him to distribute among his friends hundreds of thousands of dollars robbed from the people, a fact which he must have known because it was brought to his attention by members on this side.
Does the Minister of Customs say that he still keeps a patronage list after the disclosures made by the Cassels' Commission ?

We have very little in the way of patronage. I have no personal knowledge of the particular item in question, but I am informed that these are largely goods bought at different periods. These locks have to be made with keys different from other padlocks, and we have to make a special arrangement for their manufacture. However, as the question has been raised, I shall look into the matter tomorrow.
Will the hon. minister as-'certain what kind of kettles were bought at $1.75 ?
I am told that they are for testing tea in the laboratory.
You can get the very best copper kettles at $1.25 and we are paying $1.75.
There is 50 cents to be accounted for.

It is not quite enough to ask us to accept the statement that because these prices have been certified to by an experienced officer they are therefor all right, because when we examined into the purchases for the ice-breaker ' Montcalm ' and found cups and saucers charged at over $1 a piece, and the prices certified to as fair and reasonable we ascertained afterwards that these charges were simply robbery. When we look through the Auditor General's account and see the large number of supplies purchased from the same firm, Charleson & Co., who supplied these locks, and many of them charged at exorbitant prices, according to the judgment of those in the .trade, we are justified in coming to the conclusion that there is something wrong. We are justified in concluding that there is something wrong and in asking that in view of the recent disclosures of the evils of the patronage system, the minister shall abandon the use of the patronage list in making purchases for his department. Charleson is on the patronage list and is able to sell goods to the department, but time after time we know that goods have been supplied by him above the market price.

For the little purchases we have to make in my department, I do not think we could adopt any other plan than our present one. I could not have more confidence in any purchasing agent than I have in our present one, and to advertise for the articles would cost five times what they are worth.
My question is, will the goods be purchased without resorting to the patronage list, will instructions be given to the purchasing agent to buy where he can get the goods at the lowest price?
I will look into the matter.
It is a question of principle, not of a few items here; it is a question of the interest of the country.
I admit that the interest of the country is supreme, but it is not in the interest of the country to go advertising1 for a few hundred dollars' worth of goods bought during the year.
I do not want him to advertise.
These purchases can all be investigated before the Public Accounts Committee.

The minister says he has a purchasing agent who has been in the service 30 years and who is perfectly honest. The rule has been that this agent has been told to go to Charleson's and purchase say tea kettles. Charleson says the price is $1.75, but at another store it would be $1.20. If the minister has allowed rake offs of 50 per cent on tea kettles that is not working in the interest of the country.

I hope he does not think I got a rake off. I did not know that anything was bought from Charleson. Certainly it was not done under my instructions. The commissioner hears what has been said and I have no doubt that he will investigate it in the morning; I will myself if I can think of it.

I do not think that is going far enough. Some of the other ministers without being asked have undertaken to
abolish the patronage list, and surely it is not too much to ask the hon. minister to do so.

You do not want to make me promise to adopt a new system1 until I find out whether it is best. Leave that to me.
Expenses of maintenance of revenue cruisers and preventive service, $30,000.
I think this jtem will have to stand, as we are referred to for the details to section 'O' of the Auditor General's Report, which we have not yet received.

I am sure my hon. friend (Mr. George Taylor) would not want this item to stand, particularly after the full discussion we have had. There is a decrease of $10,000. This steamer 'Constance ' is used in the customs preventive service in eastern waters. The Marine Department manage the vessel and we recoup them for what they do. The captain is our officer. And, as I have said, there is a decrease of $10,000. I hope the hon. gentleman will not ask that this item stand; in fact, I know he will not. Well, we will

call that carried. This next amount is also one that will commend itself to the committee.
Amount to be paid to the Department of Justice to be disbursed by and accounted for to it for secret preventive service, $5,000.
This money is required for purposes which, possibly, we may not wish to disclose. The money is at the disposal of the Justice Department. The audit is a confidential one, in which, I think, the leader of the opposition shares.

We have no objection to that item. But to the previous item, if you will look at the Auditor General's Report, page F-43, immediately after the item of the steamer ' Constance,' appears certain charges for the steamer ' Arctic,' and we are referred to page F-37 of the Auditor General's Report of 1906-7. We have not had an opportunity yet to look that up. And the charge for the * Constance ' here is $25,078.54, for which no details are given. Therefore, I think the vote should be allowed to stand. It will only take a few moments to put it through when we have had an opportunity to see the next part of the Auditor General's Report if everything is right with these amounts for the ' Constance ' and the ' Arctic.'

I hope the hon. gentleman (Mr. George Taylor) will not press that, and that any hon. member on that side who has influence with him will get him to withdraw his objection. The expenditure on the ' Arctic,' so far as we are concerned, was to pay the expenses of sending a customs officer to assert Canada's sovereignty in northern waters by collecting customs dues from the American and Scotch whalers there.
What revenue did he get?

Not much, it is true, but though it was only the hundredth part of what it cost to send the officer there, I am sure the House will agree that it was only proper to assert Canada's sovereignty in those waters.
I thought Captain Bernier did that by raising the flag?
So he did. But we sent a customs officer with him and when we send a customs officer it means something, for he gets the hard cash.
So far as I am concerned, if the minister, on some item of the Marine Department
On the supple-mentaries.
I understand that there are to be no supplementaries.
I am afraid we shall have some for this year, but I hope none for next year. I am ready to give the information at any time.

On some item of the Marine and Fisheries estimates, the Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) will allow this item to be discussed.
Post Office Department-Salaries, $488,944-Contingencies, $65,755.
On what page of the Auditor General's Report are the expenditures for last year given?
The part in which these appear is not yet printed. But this is for the inside service only.
Let the item stand. Surely the Postmaster General is not going to ask us to pass this without the report?

I do not know what special questions may be asked with regard to this. I am confident I can give all ex planations to satisfy hon. members. If this were for the outside service I could understand that there might be some difficulty, but it is for the inside service-
I would remind the Postmaster General that there are many members who never saw the Auditor General's Report, and, of course, they would like to have an opportunity to study these details.
As a matter of course, the item cannot be pressed without the Auditor General's Report if any objection is taken.

Take Public Works.
Public Works Department-Salaries, $324,800.
Contingencies, $15,000.

speakeroldname: Hon. WM. PUGSLEY (Minister of Public Works).
speechtext: Previous to the coming into effect of the present Civil Service Act, there were only 36 employees of the Public Works Department on the Civil Service list, while there were about two hundred employed, the large majority of whom were not on the permanent list. Under the new law these are now brought into the Civil Service. If hon. members will refer to page 26 of the Estimates they will see the details. The number of officers to be provided for is 237, nearly all of whom were in the employ of the department previously.
Will the minister give us a list of the appointees of the Public Works Department during the last twelve months?

I cannot do so to-night, but I should be glad to furnish it in answer to the inquiry made.
20J
Better bring down the information, and meantime let the item stand.

I think I can give the explanation. We propose providing for one additional engineer and one chief draughtsman, amounting to $4,200. In addition, we provide for an additional clerk in the third division of subdivision A, amounting to $900. Then the statutory increases for 190910, for 196 employees, amount to $5,262.50. Then we think we do well to make provision for unforeseen additional appointments' or other changes to the extent of $5,000. Then there is the balance covering the differences between the annual increases in the salaries and the increases authorized by order in council dated May 5 and August 6 and August 31 of 1908, amounting to $8,958. I have a list of the [DOT] names of all those who were in the service when the Civil Service Act came into force, also of the 196 employees who have been brought under the Civil Service Act. I will read them to the hon. gentleman if he desires.

There is an enormous increase in the vote, and I would suggest that the minister put his explanations as fully as possible upon the ' Hansard,' and then we will let the item stand and take it up to-morrow when we can see the explanations.
Won't the hon. gentleman let it go through to-night ? I will be glad to give information later on in a return.
I would be glad to accommodate the hon. gentleman, but I would prefer that he put his explanations fully upon the ' Hansard ' so that we can understand them.

I do not wish unduly to press the item, but it is early in the evening. I think I have given quite a full explanation already. In addition I have here the names of all those who were in the temporary service and who were transferred to the permanent service by virtue of the Civil Service Act. Those names I need not read to-night, because they are all embodied in the order of classification which has been brought down to the House. The hon. gentleman will find there the names and present salaries, and also salaries under the reorganization.

Generally speaking, is the increased vote due to the fact that men are placed upon the regular permanent staff who have been paid out of many other votes of different characters in the public works estimates during previous years ?

Yes. As an illustration, turn to the miscellaneous, and the hon. gen-

615
tleman will find that there are two votes alone showing substantial decreases. Take the miscellaneous vote on page 7 of the estimates. Last year there was a vote for the engineering branch of $185,000, this year we are only asking for $145,000. The reason is that the engineering staff resident in Ottawa was largely upon the temporary list, and they all go to the permanent list. In the same way, under the architectural branch, there was $65,000 last year, and we only ask for $25,000 this year. Then in the estimates of this year the temporary and non-professional branch at Ottawa amount-mg to a very large sum, is wiped out and that is what makes the difference and accounts in the largely increased amount for the Civil Service. Ihe amounts for temporary clerks are struck out altogether, and the amounts for engineering and architectural branch are reduced in the vicinity of $80,000.
Comparing this vote for 1909-10 with the vote last year covering the same items, in different forms, was there an increase or decrease, and for what amount ?

The increase would be $25,000. That is made up by the salary of the deputy minister, increased by $1,000. We provide for an assistant deputy minister at $3,000, and we are providing for an additional engineer and a draughtsman $4,200 for both, also another third class clerk. We also provide $5,000 for other increases in the staff that may be found necessary during the coming year. Then the remaining $8,958 is made up by the differences between the annual increases in the salaries and the same increases which were made by orders in council of May 5 and August 6 and 31 last.

Could you tell us offhand how much of the increase is due in the first place to additional employees, in the second place, to statutory increases, and in the third place, to increases of any other character ?
The new employees get statutory increases as well. I have just given them to my hon. friend.
What is contemplated by the provision of $5,000 P

It is contemplated possibly there may be some additions to the staff required, some additional architects, and possibly some addition to the cement branch, and in the clerical staff as well. The work in the department is increasing. One might suppose from the reduction in the estimates that the work was not increasing. But I want to tell the committee that the work goes on just the same. Under the estimates provided last year the architectural branch and the engineering Mr PUGSLEY.
branch still go on making their plans and specifications, because we do not understand that the work provided for last session is being dropped, it is merely postponed. All the necessary work will have to go on in order to fulfil the policy adopted by parliament last session.

The minister has not given the figures as they are stated on page 26. He says there is an increase of 2 in the first division, and 1 in the third division. But if he will look at the second division, there were fifty-eight temporaries and eleven permanent, and he is asking for seventy-five, an increase of six in the second division. He has not stated that to the committee at all but the figures are here before us.

That would be included in the $5,000. I say that amount is for possible increases. There are a number who are not actually in the employ of the department now, but I have put in $5,000 for the purpose of covering that.
The hon. gentleman estimates 75 at $98,000.
As against 69 before.
That increased six over last year and then my hon. friend is asking for an extra $5,000 so that he may appoint more.
In making up the $28,000 I have put in $5,000 as the possible amount which may be required for these additional clerks.

My hon. friend is asking for 9 and there is a reduction of 2 in one of the items in the third division. There are 43 outside and 4 permanent, making 47. take 2 from your 9 new appointments and it leaves an increase in the stall of 7 in the face of a falling revenue. Then I want that information because I am informed that just before the Civil Service Act took effect there was a large number added to the staff.
There were no additions to the staff just before the Civil Service Act came into force.
There were a number of employees added to the force; I do not know whether you call it the staff or not. Then I want the names of the new appointees.

I think my hon. friend is entirely in error. Possibly he may have in his mind that some additional labourers may have been employed, but there were no additions to the staff just before the Civil Service Act came into force.

Does the transfer from the outside to the inside service mean a change of occupation or residence?

61ff
PUGSLEY. No. In the Public Works Department there was an organization of what was known as the temporary non-professional class. Away back in the time of Sir Hector Langevin this system was adopted. The number of those who were in the civil service was very small as compared with the temporary appointments. That system was carried right on until the Civil Service Act came into force on the 1st September and which brought all these into the permanent service. It does not mean any change in the employment at all and they have been brought in at the salaries which they had been receiving before the 1st September.

I think we will take the minister's statement and look it over, and possibly it may obviate any further discussion. Let the item stand and we will look over the statement.
Item allowed to stand.
What item shall we take
I think we had better adjourn now.

It is very early to ad-.journ. Had we not better take up public buildings chargeable to capital?
Ottawa Astronomical (Observatory-additional buildings, etc., $14,000.

This vote of $14,000 is asked to make provision for the construe-tion of a residence for the chief astronomer and also to complete coelostat house and standardizing hut in connection with the astronomical observatory. The proposed building to be occupied by the chief astronomer is to be a brick building with a stone toundation two and a half stories in height. The residence of the chief astronomer will cost about $16,000. As a great deal of the work of the chief astronomer has to be done at night it is necessary that he should have his residence close to the observatory. The vote of last year was $23,000, and we are now asking for $14,000 to finish the work.
Has the contract been let?
The contract for the residence has not been let.
Has the $23,000 been expended?
Not all. There was a contract for a coelostat hut and standardizing hut at $13,900, besides which there was the cost of heating, electric wiring, etc.

I thought that $23,000 was voted for the new building under contract?
. Mr. PUGSLEY. It was voted for the standardizing hut and the new coelostat
house, the contract for which was $13,900, heating apparatus $1,000, electric wiring, $500, etc.
To whom was the contract for the building let?

To Messrs. John O'Leary
and M. J. Whelan, of Ottawa, the lowest tenderers. Messrs Doran & Devlin were the lowest tenderers for the residence.
Were public tenders asked for the residence ?
Yes, and five tenders received'.
Where is this residence going to be located?
Close to the observatory.
Is it the policy of the government to erect residences for the chief clerks?
This is a residence for the chief astronomer.
What salary does he get?
I do not know at this moment; he is an officer of the Department of the Interior. It is my duty as Minister of Public Works to provide the necessary accommodation for the chief astronomer.
Were there only two tenders for this building?
For the coelostat house and standardizing hut. These were the lowest tenderers.

I think the minister should be able to give us the salary that the chief astronomer is getting. If he is getting a large salary why should the people of Canada furnish him with a $15,000 residence? We have had instances in this House where the government have built residences for people in the service who are receiving enormous salaries. A great many of the people who pay the money have to live in small houses and paying a man a salary such as I am told the chief astronomer gets and furnishing him with a $15,000 residence is exacting more from the poor labouring classes of this country than should be exacted by any government.

Ordinarily speaking my hon friend would be entirely right. The government does not, as a rule, provide residences for its employees, but my hon. friend will see that to enable the chief astronomer to perform his work properly it is necessary that he shall be at night constantly at the observatory. The observatory is two or three miles from Ottawa and it would be very inconvenient for him to reside in Ottawa. I resisted the pressure for a considerable time, but on urgent representations made to me I felt we would have to erect a residence for Mr. King.
Is there any diminution in his salary in consideration of his getting this house free of rent.
Not that I am aware of.
What is the amount of the tender for this residence?
The lowest tender was $12,300.
Are we to understand that $15,000 will complete this residence? My experience is that these buildings cost twice their estimated cost.

This contract is for the building alone and then there will be the heating and wiring, and I assume from the information I have that $3,000 or $4,000
additional will be necessary.

Is it essential that the chief astronomer should have a residence for his family close to the observatory. Even though he has to work at night, he is not any worse off than any others in that respect, and I don't see why it is not possible to provide him with suitable quarters which will not cost anything like this enormous amount. Why should we build such an expensive residence for a high paid official when the poor labouring classes of the country have to live in huts ?

I hesitated, just as my hon. friend (Mr. Staples) would have done were he in my position, to build this residence, but there was no house close to the observatory which he could get and it would be unreasonable to ask him to build one himself. It was brought to my notice that a good many years ago a residence was erected by the Conservative govern. ment on the experimental farm_ for Dr. Saunders and for some other officials.
What did it cost?
It is a very fine residence and making allowance for difference in cost of material and labour it would be quite as expensive as this one.

The whole policy of the government seems to be to give advantages to the highly paid officials, while withholding from under-paid officials who do the greater portion of the work, that consideration to which they are entitled. I know men who are working in the Civil Service in this city for $40 and $45 a month and who are expected to rear their families on this miserable pay. But when we come to the highly paid officials the policy of the government is to increase their emoluments by leaps and bounds.

In view of the fact, that, instead of adopting the report of the commission to give a percentage on salaries which would be an advantage to the highly paid officials the government proposes Mr. PUGSLEY.
to give a flat increase of $150 to each civil servant, the criticism of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Staples) is hardly just.
This building is to be erected right under the eyes of the Department of Public Works in Ottawa with their immense staff and yet they pay Mr. John Sharp as clerk of works for 143 days at $4 per day.
Mr. Sharp is one of the staff of the Public Works Department and his services in this case are properly chargeable to that building.
I voice my protest against putting $20,000 into a building for the accommodation of any civil servant in Ottawa. I think a $10,000 house to be good enough for any man we employ.

But that is not a patch on it, for if the hon. gentleman looks at the Auditor General's Report he will find the government paid to the Office Specialty Company, (a pet company here in Ottawa established to get business from the government) $5,970 for library fittings for this building.
That is for the observatory itself and not for this residence.

The item says here: 'For fitting library steel cases, gallery and stairs, and bevelling below the gallery, $5,970.' I want to draw attention to another item on the same page. E. P. McGrath & Co. have supplied 182 lineal feet oak for transit house at 15c. per lineal foot; two inside doors with fan lights, and two pine door frames with fan light and oak door, with locks, &c., supplied and set up, $132.15.' Just fancy $61 per frame door with a fan light in it. Were these bought by tender?
Mr, PUGSLEY. My hon. friend will see that the first item is for fittings for the library, steel cases, gallery and stairs and panelling below the gallery, less the amount of $970 paid the previous year. In the laboratory there is a library because there must be various works which are of great importance to the chief astronomer. There must also be records of his observations from night to night, which must be preserved, and it is not improper that they should be kept in steel fittings so as to make the inside of the building as fire proof as possible. Then the stairway from the bottom to the upper gallery must be of iron, as they are in all large libraries. This was let by tender. There are only two firms which make these fittings in Canada, and tenders were received from the two.
Is there a library also provided in the residence?
Not that I am aware of.

Will there be a man employed in that building as caretaker?
_ Mr. PUGSLEY. I don't propose to furnish a caretaker.
Are the two firms from which the hon. gentleman asked tenders on the patronage list?

There are only two firms in Canada where these goods can be got. One is in Ottawa, and the other is in a city in western Ontario. Before purchasing, a very careful examination was made of the fittings made in the United States, and used generally in the public offices in Washington and the different state capitals, and the chief architect ascertained that the prices asked us were fair and reasonable.
In view of the strong condemnation of the patronage list by the Civil Service Commission, does the hon. gentleman propose to abolish it ?

I have given instructions to abolish it as far as possible, and' invite public tenders. I am now considering the establishing of a purchasing department, as the Minister of Marine and Fisheries has done, in accordance with the report of the Civil Service Commission, but that organization will take a little time and the person in charge of that branch will have to be thoroughly experienced and reliable.
How comes it that the hon. minister paid $2.50 per barrel for 85 barrels of cement bought from Kirby & Co., when he could buy that cement at Hull for $1.80?

That was but a small
quantity and no tenders were called for.
You could purchase it by retail at $1.65. I see the familiar name of Chas. Patton down for four fire extinguishers at $15 a piece, or two more than last year.
Last year the order may have been a large one and $15 is a reasonable price, for they are very good articles.
Does this item include the furnishings for that house as well as the building?
No.
What is the necessity for such a large house? Has the gentleman a large family or does he expect to, or are other gentlemen going to live with him?
Does the minister propose to furnish the house?

I have no intention to ask for such a vote. That might properly he done by Dr. King himself.
